en: The *Tantrarahasya*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Rāmānuja.
May Viṣṇu, dwelling in Dharmapura, protect you—he who, assuming the form of Narasiṃha, sat upon a lotus throne facing the east while gazing at the Godāvarī river before him. || 1 ||
Situated on the bank of the Godāvarī, the great City of Dharma shines resplendent;
there, I remember in my heart the station of Viṣṇu, who has descended in the form of Nṛsiṃha. || 2 ||
I bow to the sage Jaimini, by whom the Mīmāṃsā consisting of twelve chapters was composed in aphorisms for the sake of establishing the intended meaning of the Vedas.
May that Śabarasvāmin be victorious, renowned across various Vedic branches, who composed a commentary (bhāṣya) in order to clarify the meaning of the Sūtras. (4)
Having considered the power of the words and the power of the meaning of the Śrutis,
he composed two commentaries, the Bṛhatī and the Laghū.
Victorious in the three worlds is this very teacher Prabhākara, who composed a concise commentary upon the profound [Brahma-sūtra] Bhāṣya. || 5 ||
Likewise, Śālikānātha composed the *Ṛjuvimalā* and the *Dīpaśikhā*, respectively, as extensive and concise commentaries upon the *Pañcikā*, clarifying its meaning. (6)
Likewise, Śālikanātha diligently composed another work consisting of various chapters, titled the *Pañcikā*, for the purpose of distinguishing between the means and objects of knowledge.
But Bhavanātha, condensing the two commentaries and the *Pañcikās*, composed the universally esteemed treatise known as the *Nayaviveka*. (8)
Diverse in some respects and non-different in others, likewise both contradictory and non-contradictory in one place—
the two Tantras, along with the instruction on the secret of the Tantras, are here expanded according to the method taught by the Guru.

I shall here summarize, in concise words and according to the principles of the Guru’s Tantras, the determination of the reality of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and the knower, which has been elaborated upon in my previous works, for the pleasure of the learned. (10)

Experience (*anubhūti*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the conventional usage of "means of valid cognition" applies only to that among investigators. Furthermore, experience is consciousness distinct from memory. Memory is knowledge produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), because the conventional usage of "memory" applies only to that. In this definition, the inclusion of the term "impression" excludes cognitions such as perception, since those arise solely from the sense organs and other such factors. The inclusion of the term "solely" (*mātra*) excludes recognition, since that arises from the sense organ assisted by an impression.
The distinction between memory and experience will be elaborated upon later.

But surely, even memory is, according to your own view, in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*). Why then is it not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? True—it is not conformity with reality that is the cause of validity, for that is common to all cognitions. Rather, it is the state of being a direct experience (*anubhūtitva*) alone. Memory, however, despite possessing that [conformity], is distinct from direct experience because it is produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, by apprehending an object previously experienced as "that," it does not determine the object independently; thus, it is not a means of valid knowledge.

Even a valid cognition (*pramā*) that is a memory deficient in its partial aspects is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) solely because it is produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), even though it lacks dependence on another [cognition] for its own apprehension. For this very reason, because they lack both types of dependence, successive cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-vittayaḥ*) remain valid knowledge even when they apprehend what has already been apprehended.

How is truthfulness common [to all cognition]? Because it is restricted by the fact that every cognition is non-deviant from its object. But how can there be non-deviation? For there exist error, such as "this is silver" or "the conch is yellow," doubt, such as "is it a post or a person? and dreams, which are not [in accordance with reality]. Furthermore, the cognition of silver determines the very mother-of-pearl standing before one as being silver.

Furthermore, if [the cognition] had silver alone as its object, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form "this is silver. Also, one who seeks silver would not engage with the mother-of-pearl fragment lying before him, because there is a rule that comprehension and purposeful activity must have the same object. In the same way, cognitions such as "the conch is yellow" are also of the nature of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*).

Furthermore, if all cognition were equally "in accordance with reality" (*yāthārthya*), from what source would the distinction between error and non-error arise? For that distinction is based precisely on being either in accordance with reality or not. And from what source would there be sublation (*bādha*) in the form of the thought "this is not [so]"? For sublation is characterized by the withdrawal of an object previously apprehended, and such withdrawal is impossible if [the cognition] is in accordance with reality.
It is replied: In whatever cognition a certain object appears, that alone is its object, and nothing else; for that [object]...

Because it does not appear therein; for if that which does not appear were the object, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the appearance of one thing as another is indeed contrary to experience. Consequently, in this case, the cognition of silver does not have the mother-of-pearl as its object, because the latter does not appear therein; rather, it has silver as its object alone.

[Objection: If that is so, how is the presentation of the qualified object "this is silver" with respect to the thing standing before one accounted for? [Reply: It is as follows—first, when there is contact between the sense organ and the object, the mere mother-of-pearl, whose specific attributes have not been grasped, is apprehended in a general way as "this. Subsequently, due to a defect, the mere silver, which resembles it but is deficient in certain respects, is remembered. In the world, it is indeed observed that the sight of a similar thing produces the memory of a similar thing. And that memory, because of the loss of its specific elements, takes on a form identical to direct experience.

To this extent, there is no dispute between us. In that regard, due to the non-apprehension of the difference between the perceived and the remembered, or between the perception and the memory, there is merely a linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) based on the apprehension of a general form (*sāmānyākāra*), but not a cognition of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭadhī*). For that very reason, purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) is also justified. Furthermore, when the difference is apprehended at a later time, the sublation (*bādha*) consisting in the failure of the linguistic usage is also logically established. And that [sublation] does not involve the removal of the object of the prior cognition, because both [the prior cognition and the subsequent one] are in accordance with reality; rather, it is simply the failure of the linguistic usage.

Knowledge is indeed not sublated, because it corresponds to reality; rather, it is practical activity (*vyavahāra*) that is sublated. Even the sublation discussed in the investigation of the tenth chapter pertains only to practical activity, and not to knowledge itself. For in that context, only the performance of threshing upon *kṛṣṇala* beans and the grinding of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) are sublated, but not the cognition of their status as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), since that cognition is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). From this very fact follows the distinction between the correct and the false: where there is a discrepancy with practical activity, the prior cognition is erroneous; but where there is no such discrepancy, it is correct.

Objection: In cases such as "hot water," "the cool moonbeam," or "heavy gold," would there not be correctness due to the non-contradiction of worldly practice? Reply: No, because even in those instances, the cognition is based on the non-apprehension of difference. Although its erroneous nature exists, it is not treated as such in practical discourse.

[Objection: Granted that this "this-ness" (idam-aṃśa) may be an experience, but how can the "silver-ness" (rajata-aṃśa) be a memory? [Reply: Because of the loss of the "that-ness" (tattā-aṃśa). For the cognition "that" does not arise there; therefore, it is more appropriate to regard it as an experience. [Reply: True, but it is not a visual experience, because there is no contact with the eyes. Nor is it an inference, due to the absence of a logical mark (liṅga). By elimination, it is indeed a memory. The loss of its "that-ness," however, is due to the influence of a defect (doṣa). For this very reason, even among common people...

In that regard, the conventional usage is based on direct experience; however, for investigators, it is otherwise. Since its object is merely the mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—even though it lacks the sense of "that-ness" (*tattā*)—it is also distinguished from a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhika*).

But could it not be that even visual perception, due to a defect (*doṣa*), is simply a specific type of experience? It could not be so. Defects merely obstruct the innate capacity for an effect; they do not produce a distinct or different kind of effect. Indeed, even from a rice seed (*śālibīja*) crowded with a thousand defects, a barley sprout does not arise. Furthermore, even you, who advocate the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), have first admitted the existence of perception and recollection, and only then accepted that error arises from those two.

For this very reason, your conventional usage here is that there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of what is being remembered. For us, however, since the designation of "error" (*bhrānti*) is established and the occurrence of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) is possible through those two [the memory and the perception] themselves when their difference is not grasped, we do not accept a third cognition; this is due to parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore, the violation of the rule that [cognition] must correspond to reality (*yāthārthya*) is an additional defect in this case.

[Objection: Is it not the case that activity occurs only toward that which is the object of a cognition? And the cognition of silver does not have the mother-of-pearl as its object; therefore, how can there be activity toward it? [Reply: True, that is exactly so in the case of a real piece of silver. But here, however, [activity] is based solely on the non-apprehension of difference. Furthermore, you yourself must admit the non-apprehension of difference in this instance; otherwise, no error would arise. For an error does not arise when the specific difference is apprehended, since such apprehension is the very thing that prevents it.

For this very reason, your inference—"the fragment of mother-of-pearl is the object of the cognition of silver, because it is the objective of the activity of one seeking silver, like real silver"—is refuted. In that case [of real silver], there is non-discrepancy; here, however, it is not so, because of discrepancy. Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the two terms of your proposition, like saying "the word 'pot' denotes a cloth" or "the eye perceives odor."

Furthermore, if cognition were to deviate from its object, the form being perceived would necessarily be restricted to cognition alone; consequently, all cognition would become endowed with a form, resulting in a confusion with the tenets of the externalist schools.

Likewise, even the cognition of a yellow conch is indeed valid. To explain: when the clear bile-substance present in the eye goes out along with its rays, the yellowness residing therein is perceived here [in the conch]. Likewise, the conch itself is perceived as possessing that defect. There is no rule that a substance and its quality must always be perceived together; rather, although there is a mutual expectancy between them, their existing lack of connection is not cognized. Consequently, due to the non-apprehension of that lack of connection in that case, there occurs the linguistic usage based on a qualified cognition. Activity also proceeds from that very same cause.

Even in the cognition of two moons, due to defects such as pressing with a finger, the visual ray—which is divided from the moon—produces duality in a single moon. Therein, because of the non-apprehension of the non-connection between the duality and the moon, there arises the conventional usage "two moons. Similarly, in the case of a firebrand-stick (*alātadaṇḍa*) moving very rapidly in all directions, cognitions arise in immediate succession; therein, due to the non-apprehension of the intervals, there occurs the cognition and conventional usage of a "wheel" (*cakra*). Thus, the conventional usage of a wheel applies to the firebrand. Likewise, the visual ray falling upon a mirror first perceives the mirror along with its specific qualities.

But subsequently, being struck back, it returns merely as a reflection. Therein, due to the non-apprehension of the difference between the mirror and the face, there is the conventional usage of "face" with respect to the mirror. And due to the non-apprehension of the difference between the properties residing therein—such as leftness, rightness, largeness, and smallness—and those of the face, there is the conventional usage of those locations and so forth with respect to the face.

Dream, however, is nothing but memory; for it does not arise with respect to what has not been previously experienced. Due to a defect (*doṣa*), there is a loss of the sense of "that-ness" (*tattā*). Furthermore, by the power of unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), the form of grasping [the object] and the fact that the objects have been experienced are not determined [as such]. A particular state [of consciousness] and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) are the awakeners of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). For this very reason, the cognition of one who is awake is of exactly the same nature.

Likewise, doubt (*saṃśaya*) is not a single cognition; rather, these two are of the nature of memory, having as their objects the states of being a post and being a person, with the aspect of "that-ness" (*tattā*) removed, arising from the perception of a vertical object standing before one and being mutually exclusive of each other. All of this is indeed real (*yathārtha*).

Since neither of those two distinct features can be established when they are mutually excluded within a substrate standing before one, the person who intends to initiate a settled linguistic convention is unable to do so and thus falls into doubt; hence, there arises the conventional usage of doubt. Furthermore, if some cognition were to deviate from its object, then by suspecting that all cognitions are likewise unreliable, there would be no confidence in the world.

If it is objected: "Even in your own view, when there is non-apprehension of difference as the basis for activity despite some manifestation, and when there is a failure of practical efficacy (*vyavahāra-visaṃvāda*), then because of the suspicion that this might be the case everywhere, a lack of confidence remains just as it was," we reply: No, because of the disparity. For when truthfulness is common, there is a natural confidence everywhere that "whatever is manifested is real," and activity is likewise natural. Any lack of confidence that arises in certain instances is removed with little effort.

Because, when there is no discrepancy in subsequent practical activity (*vyavahāra*), one ascertains that the preceding cognition had as its object a specific entity; whereas in the case of discrepancy, one merely ascertains that the objects were those various things whose distinctions were grasped, being entirely devoid of mutual connection.

Therefore, all knowledge is in accordance with reality. Even though it is in accordance with reality, memory is not a valid means of knowledge; it is established that direct experience alone is a valid means of knowledge.

The Teachers (Ācāryas), however, have formulated the general definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "A cognition that is firm, non-contradictory, and apprehends what has not been previously apprehended is a *pramāṇa*. Furthermore, they have established that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), whereas invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). As it has been said:
"Therefore, let that cognition which, having arisen with firmness, does not encounter contradiction by another cognition, be recognized as a *pramāṇa*."

Thus it is said. And his disciples have elaborated upon that self-validity (svatastva) in many ways. For instance, some there have explained it as follows: this word "sva" (self) signifies "one's own"; "prāmāṇyam" (validity) is the correspondence of the object with reality; and the word "jāyate" (is born) is supplied by implication. Consequently, the meaning is this: validity, characterized as the correspondence of the object with reality, is produced from its own cause alone, and not from excellences (guṇas), because the latter serve only to counteract defects (doṣas).

If validity were dependent upon qualities (*guṇa*), then because the Veda is not of human origin and thus lacks the qualities of a speaker, it would possess no validity. Invalidity, which is distinct from this [validity], does not arise from its own cause, but rather from a defect (*doṣa*); thus, invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). For this very reason, in cases such as "this is silver," the aspect of "this" possesses intrinsic validity due to its own cause, whereas the falsity of the "silver" aspect arises from a defect.
This view does not accord with the treatises of the Teacher, and for that reason it has been disregarded by his own followers.

Others, however, maintain: this word *sva* (self) refers to the cognition itself. Validity (*prāmāṇya*) is the ascertainment of an object as it truly is, which was not previously apprehended. Therefore, such validity arises from the cognition's own nature (*svarūpa*), and not from the cognition of excellences (*guṇa*) or from the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), on the other hand, arises extrinsically (*parataḥ*) from the cognition of defects (*doṣa*) or from the cognition that the object is otherwise than it appears. This position too has been rejected by those very same [Buddhists]. In that regard, first of all, it is logical that invalidity arises extrinsically.

For the invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) of the cognition of silver is not produced by the cognition of a defect or the like, because it is invalid precisely at the moment of its arising. Invalidity consists in the determination of an object as being other than what it actually is. And that [invalidity] occurs in an invalid cognition spontaneously (*svataḥ*); it does not depend on a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*) or the like. For a cognition that is valid at the time of its arising is not subsequently rendered invalid by a subverting cognition; rather, the invalidity already known at the time of arising is merely made manifest later by a subverting cognition. Furthermore, it is also illogical for validity (*prāmāṇya*) itself to have a spontaneous birth.

If by "from itself" (*svataḥ*) one intends merely the nature of cognition (*jñānasvarūpa*), then even false cognition would possess intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇya*), since the nature of cognition is no different there as well. If, on the other hand, correct cognition is intended, then it would follow that the arising of validity occurs from a valid cognition; in that case, there would be the production of something from itself, because validity is non-different from the nature of correct cognition.

Others, however, maintain that the word "own" (*sva*) refers to the cognition itself, and the phrase "it appears by virtue of its fitness" (*yogyatayā ca bhāti*) is supplied as an ellipsis. Thus, validity residing in that cognition is made known [by the cognition itself], whereas invalidity is understood from external sources. This too has been refuted by those very same [authorities]. For a cognition does not grasp itself or its own validity, because it is exhausted solely by the apprehension of the object. Indeed, once a cognition has arisen, it does not appear such that one thinks, "I am a valid means of knowledge," or "My validity exists."

Cognition alone is postulated because the manifestation of an object would otherwise be inexplicable; its validity as well is derived from that very same source. Therefore, the claim that it "shines forth by itself" (is self-evident) is untenable.

But those who know the true doctrine of the Teacher [Prabhākara] maintain: this word *sva* (self) refers to the self (*ātman*). Validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in being possessed of an object (*arthavattva*). And the word "shines forth" (*bhāti*) is supplied as an ellipsis. Thus, the meaning is that validity—characterized by the correspondence of the object—is manifested from the very nature of the cognition itself; in other words, the capacity of mere cognition to illuminate the reality of the object is innate. As it has been stated by his followers: "This word *sva* denotes the self; validity shines forth by itself. And the 'being thus' (*tathābhāva*) of the object is proclaimed to be validity."

The intrinsic validity (*autsargika-prāmāṇya*) is as follows: that which constitutes the suchness of the object and by virtue of which cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—the manifestation of that [object] shines forth from its own nature alone, and not from the cognition of a quality (*guṇa*), the cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), or the cognition of correspondence (*saṃvāda*). Invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), characterized by the object being otherwise than it appears, does not shine forth intrinsically; rather, it is established as extrinsic (*parataḥ*), arising either from the cognition of a defect in the causes or from a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*) such as "this is not so. As the Teachers have said: "Therefore, intrinsic validity is established everywhere as the general rule;
it is set aside by the cognition of a subverting factor or by the cognition of a defect in the causes."

Thus [it is said]. "Established" (sthita) means attained or accepted—that is to say, [established]. "Everywhere" (sarvatra) means not only in the case of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but in the case of all knowledge whatsoever; for this inquiry does not concern only cognitions that are means of valid cognition, since [otherwise] the status of being the general rule (*autsargikatva*) would not hold. What, then, are those [cognitions] distinct from doubt and recollection? Since the invalidity of those two is evident, they are not [included].

[The two views] are within the scope of investigation. If this inquiry were conducted with reference to cognitions produced by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then their intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) alone would have been established. In that case, since the Veda lacks validity as admitted by both parties, it would not be the subject of the inquiry; consequently, an inquiry irrelevant to its validity would be unnecessary, like an examination of a crow’s teeth.

However, when intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) has been established on the basis of cognition alone, the validity of the Veda is also generally attained; since there is an absence of defects in its causes and so forth, it is free from exception. Thus, validity is the general rule (*autsargika*), while anything else is an exception (*āpavādika*). This [treatise] would therefore have a purpose.

[Objection: If validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in the correspondence of the object with reality (*arthatathātva*), then that [validity] would follow for memory as well, since by it too there is an ascertainment of reality. [Reply: Not so. In common worldly usage, validity is intended to be a triad: (1) the non-recollection of [the object] as already apprehended, (2) the reality of the object, and (3) the capacity of the cognition to produce an ascertainment regarding that [object]. It is precisely in these cases that the term "means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) is applied. Therefore, memory does not possess validity.

Thus, this is the summary of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final position (uttarapakṣa) here: since the cognition of a jar is observed to arise from the word "jar," the jar is difficult to ascertain by means of mere cognition—which is common to both the existence and non-existence of the jar. Therefore, there is no ascertainment of its validity (*prāmāṇya*) intrinsically (*svataḥ*). Rather, its ascertainment occurs through the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), through corroboration (*saṃvāda*), or through the cognition of causes possessed of excellence (*guṇavat-kāraṇajñāna*). The cognition of purposeful action is intrinsically valid because it is non-deviant. Corroboration also occurs precisely because of the actual state of the object; likewise for excellence.
Therefore, the determination of validity arises solely from something else and not intrinsically; this is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is this: cognition does not determine an object by means of non-deviation or certainty; rather, it does so by its own nature (*svataḥ*). If it were unable to determine it by its own nature, then the determination of objects would be absolutely impossible, and the entire world would fall into blindness. For an object that is not determined by itself cannot be determined by another either, since the other [cognition] would likewise lack the capacity as before.

Just as the cognition of a jar is seen even when no jar exists and is therefore non-conclusive, so too the cognition of causal efficiency is seen even in the state of dreaming where that efficiency does not exist; thus, it cannot be determined by anyone. The determination of a jar through such [efficiency] is far from possible. Likewise, what is called "corroboration" (saṃvāda) is merely another cognition regarding that same object; what distinction is there between this and the previous cognition, such that what was undetermined by the former could be determined by the latter? Similarly, even from the cognition of a quality, the quality itself cannot be determined, let alone the validity of the prior cognition.

Therefore, validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), whereas invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), arising either from the cognition of defects or from a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*). In the case of the Veda, however, because of the absence of defects, the intrinsically attained validity is well-established; thus, the inquiry into its validity is purposeful as it serves that very purpose.

In this regard, the general definition [of valid cognition] is first untenable, because there is no object to be excluded by the first two terms since doubt and error possess objective reality (*yathārthya*). Furthermore, it is not pervasive of the final term, as continuous streams of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-pramā*) are excluded. Likewise, independence (*svātantrya*) is untenable, because validity is conditioned solely by the nature of being an experience (*anubhūtitva*). Similarly, extrinsicness (*paratastva*) is untenable, because invalidity is conditioned solely by the fact of being produced merely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, if validity consists in the correspondence with reality (*arthatathātva*), then it would follow that even memory possesses such validity. If you argue that the lack of non-reconnection (*ananusandhāna*) is the determinant factor, then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of recognition following a lapse of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*) and under-extension (*avyāpti*) to other cases. If you claim that being produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) is the criterion, then that alone would apply everywhere; what then is the point of the distinction between whether [validity] is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*)?

Regarding what was stated—that intrinsic validity (*svārasika-prāmāṇya*) is the primary state while extrinsic invalidity (*apavādika*) is the exception—what is meant by "intrinsic" (*svārasikatva*)? If it means the very nature of cognition, then there is the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this definition to memory (*smṛti*). If, on the other hand, it means the nature of cognition as distinct from that [memory], then we have no dispute. As for the second position, what constitutes the exception (*apavāda*)? If it is a defect (*doṣa*), its function is merely to obstruct the innate capacity [of cognition], not to be the cause of invalidity itself. If, finally, it means being produced solely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), then likewise there is no dispute.

The validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the Veda is established simply by its independence (*anapekṣatva*); what is the use of the laborious inquiry as to whether it is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*)? It was determined in the first chapter (*adhyāya*) that the Veda is a means of valid knowledge precisely because it does not depend on other means of cognition. Among those [arguments], invalidity arising from external causes—characterized by dependence (*sāpekṣatva*)—is refuted in the *Tarkapāda*. However, the invalidity arising from the suspicion of mutual non-connection (*ananvaya*) among sentences is refuted in the [remaining] three chapters (*tripādī*). Furthermore, the correspondence of cognition with reality (*jñānayāthārthya*) has been established by Śālikānātha in the *Nayavīthī* within the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*.

[Objection: But in your own view, since even memory possesses the nature of experience (*anubhūti*) with respect to its own self and the self [of the object], how can its exclusion [from experience] serve as its definition? Nor is it correct to say that only the cognized portion (*vedyāṃśa*) constitutes [experience] because it is produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), for this would not contradict [the status of] the other portions as well. Furthermore, it is contradictory for one and the same thing to possess both the nature of memory and the nature of experience. Moreover, dependence upon an [original] experience is common to all three portions. [Reply: It is said: For we do not deny the mode of apprehension (*pratītiprakāra*).

The establishment of reality is thus logical. This is its manner: whatever cognition there may be, whether in the form of perception or recollection, in all such cases the self (*ātman*) manifests directly. For if that [self] were not manifesting, objects would not appear. Indeed, every cognition is of the form "I know this"; for no consciousness whatsoever can arise without the mention of a substratum. If it were otherwise, the consequence would follow that there would be no distinction between one's own awareness and the awareness of another.

Furthermore, if [cognition] were to have other conditions as its object, there would be no rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) regarding the two objects of cognition; however, that rule is possible when they are within the scope of a single cognition. Therefore, by the very force of experience, one must accept that every cognition, in its own subjective aspect (*ātmāṃśa*), has the form of direct experience (*anubhavākāra*) and is characterized by immediate intuition (*sākṣātkāravat*). Likewise, it shines forth as self-evident even in its own subjective aspect. Since even the two objects of cognition, which are not themselves of the nature of luminosity, shine forth through their connection with it, it is that [cognition] which shines forth in such a manner.

Even though the object and the means of knowledge are devoid of any formal characteristics (*aprakārātmaka*), since their manifestation occurs through a certain relation, what else could be required for the manifestation of that [relation] itself? Nor is there any further manifestation [of a second light] at the time when the object is manifested by it; nor is it the case that [the relation] does not appear at that time, for if it were not manifest, it would follow that nothing at all would be manifest. Furthermore, objects do not become manifest in the absence of a manifesting light. By this, the argument stated by others is refuted, as they say:
"Just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself by itself, so too cognition cannot know itself by its own part."

Thus [it is said]. In this regard, is the intended contradiction that between the object and the agent, or is it the contradiction between that which illuminates an object and its own self-illumination? Not the first, because we do not accept it; for we do not admit that knowledge stands in the relation of object and agent with respect to itself. Nor the second, because it is established by the force of direct experience. For this very reason, the eternally inferable nature of knowledge as maintained by them is also refuted.

Furthermore, the object alone cannot be the inferential mark (liṅga) for that [cognition], because there is no rule of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva-niyama) between the two. Nor can it be an excellence (atiśaya) residing in the object produced by that [cognition]—which is synonymous with "knownness" (jñātatā) or "manifestness" (prākaṭya)—because there is a lack of evidence for such a thing. The designation "the jar is known" is accounted for simply by the relation to cognition. By this, the view that cognition is accessible through mental perception (mānasapratyakṣa), like pleasure and so forth, is also refuted.

Therefore, by the very force of cognition itself, it must be accepted that every cognition—which is self-luminous and necessarily possesses the form of experience regarding both the self and its own objective portion—is characterized by direct perception and constitutes valid knowledge; this applies specifically to the objective portion alone.

The status of being memory (*smṛti*), direct experience (*anubhūti*), perception (*pratyakṣa*), indirect cognition (*parokṣa*), valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*) is thus established. To explain: in whatever object-part is represented as "that" (*tad*), that part—being born of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—constitutes memory, indirect cognition, and invalid cognition. Indeed, it is logical that the state of being born of a latent impression belongs to that very part [of the object], as is observed in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

Regarding memory and dreams, although they lack the verbal reference "that" (*tad-ity-ullekha*), it has been stated above that their being produced from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) is established by elimination (*pariśeṣa*), due to the absence of sensory contact. Just as in your view—which maintains the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*)—even when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is identical, the portion consisting of the silver is produced by defects, is false, and is defective; whereas the portion consisting of "this" (*idam-aṃśa*) is true, non-defective, and produced without defects, because if that [portion] were likewise [defective], there would be the consequence of its sublation just like the other part; so too here, the distribution of properties among the parts would occur through a difference in causes.

For instance: where the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*) is delineated as "this" (*idam*), there it is perception (*pratyakṣatva*) because it arises from sense-object contact; where, however, there is no such delineation, there it is indirect (*parokṣatva*) and yet remains a form of experience (*anubhūtitva*) because it is produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*) or a word (*śabda*). Where, moreover, there is the delineation as "that" (*tad*), there it is memory (*smṛtitva*) because it arises solely from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Thus, everything is logically consistent. In all cases, the postulation of a cause is in accordance with the effect, and not otherwise.

Therefore, even when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is identical, a difference in the intermediate causes must be admitted to account for the difference in the effects. Thus it is established that experience (*anubhūti*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that experience is consciousness distinct from memory (*smṛti*). Furthermore, memory is defined as knowledge produced solely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Other definitions have also been presented and refuted in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*. We do not apply ourselves to those matters with extreme rigor, as our endeavor is restricted solely to the investigation of the meaning of the Vedas.
And that [means of valid cognition] is fivefold, distinguished as perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), and verbal testimony (*śabda*).

In this context, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is immediate cognition. Immediacy (*sākṣāttva*) consists of non-mediacy (*aparokṣya*) and vivid manifestation (*viśadāvabhāsa*). This [immediacy] is a specific property established by one's own experience, distinct from mediacy (*pārokṣya*), which serves as the basis for the direct linguistic usage regarding all cognitions in respect to their two components—the self (*ātman*) and the object itself (*svātmāṃśa*). Furthermore, in sensory cognitions, it is a specific property that pervades the three components [of subject, object, and cognition] and is the cause of direct practical activity. However, "cognition produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object" is not the definition [of perception], because it fails to apply to the two components—the self and the object—within memory (*smṛti*).

In memory as well, both components appear directly, just as they do in sensory perception; therefore, the definition is simply that dharma is that which is the direct cause of practical activity (*vyavahāra*).

Now, what is that property (*dharma*) like? It cannot be "immediacy" (*āparokṣya*), because that very [property] is yet unestablished, as it is the object under investigation. Nor can it be "being produced by the senses" (*indriyajātva*), because that does not escape the defects mentioned previously. Nor can it be "exceeding memory and inferential knowledge," because even in those cases, the portions consisting of the self and its own nature possess immediacy. It is said in reply: It is a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) which, in each of these three components [of cognition], serves as the cause for immediate practical activity (*tātkālikavyavahāra*). For in inference and the like, no immediate practical activity is observed regarding the portion of the object known (*vedyāṃśa*); this is because it is impossible for them to have past or future things as their objects.

You too must accept a property (*dharma*) that regulates the worldly, well-established conventions of the perceptible and the imperceptible; for without a regulating factor, such regulated convention is impossible. If you say, "Then let us accept such a property," we reply: it is merely a specific sub-genus within the category of cognition (*jñāna*). Do not say so; for a genus cannot exist among qualities (*guṇa*). We shall refute the possibility of its existence within the entire range of objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Or, even if it were possible:

Nevertheless, what is that which manifests it? For it is your own established tenet (*rāddhānta*) that universals (*jāti*), as they are well-known to investigators, depend upon a manifestor for their own cognition. If you say it is "being produced by a sense organ" (*indriyajanyatva*), no; for this would fail to apply (*avyāpti*) to the knowledge of God (*īśvarajñāna*), which you yourself accept [as existing]. If you say it is "conformity with the linguistic usage of 'this' (*idam*)," no; for this would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to the knowledge of a yogin regarding past and future objects. Therefore, the very method we have stated is your only refuge.

In that regard, perception, which has the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*) as its domain, is of two kinds, distinguished as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Among these, the former has the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as its object. To explain: immediately following the contact of the sense organ, first there arises a cognition consisting of the mere essential nature regarding substance, quality, and genus. And the object of that [cognition] is not merely the substance, because both genus and quality also appear [in it]. Therefore, since everything capable [of being perceived] is [present], non-conceptual perception has the essential nature as its object. The other, however, has the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) as its object. To explain:

In the state of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), because it is devoid of the synthesis of other factors, neither the persistence (*anuvṛtti*) nor the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of a universal (*jāti*) is perceived. However, in the state of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), when there is such synthesis, the perception of the persistence of the universal occurs through the recollection of its prior form. Thus, there arises a qualified cognition: "This is a jar; this too is a jar, and not a cloth. The same applies to the perception of qualities (*guṇa*). Previously, in the absence of such synthesis, the distinction between substance and quality as the excluded (*vyāvartya*) and the excluder (*vayāvartaka*) was not perceived.

In the state of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-daśā*), however, the connection of the quality with the qualified object (*guṇin*) and its distinction from others are perceived only subsequently; thus, there is the possibility of a determinate perception such as "the jar is white, not black. Therefore, conceptual cognition has a qualified object as its domain. Action, [on the other hand, is] not [of this nature].

It is the domain of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), because it is always inferable. For motion is inferred through a succession of conjunctions and disjunctions; once that [motion] has been inferred, the possibility of a subsequent qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratīti*) arises. Even in the conceptual construction of the name "Devadatta goes," the remembered word is the qualifier, since the denoted object is perceived. There is no rule that a qualifier must be apprehended solely through perception, for it is possible for it to be apprehended by another means of valid cognition as well.

Therefore, although the name and the action themselves are not directly perceived, when they are apprehended through other means of valid cognition, they serve as causes for a qualified cognition; thus, perception is of two kinds.

As for the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*): when the word *pramāṇa* is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*), as in "the act of cognizing is the means of valid cognition," then direct perception (*sākṣātkāri*) is the means of valid cognition, and the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, and indifference arising immediately thereafter are the result. When it is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), as in "that by which something is cognized is the means of valid cognition," then the required instrument—whether the internal organ (*manas*), the sense faculty, or the contact between them—is the means, while in all cases, knowledge itself is the result; for the instrument functions solely for the sake of that [knowledge].

Even in the view that [pramāṇa] is established as a state (bhāvasādhana), although valid cognition (pramā) is itself indeed the instrument with respect to the cognitions of abandonment and so forth, nevertheless, the distinction between the two positions should be understood as being intended to differentiate between knowledge and ignorance.
________ || Now, inference (anumāna).

Inference (*anumāna*) is the thorough cognition of one part, which is doubted, by means of another part, through the known necessity of their relationship, both parts residing in a single substratum. As it has been said:
"Inference is the cognition of another part, when the relationship of necessity is known, arising from the perception of one part, provided there is no sublation."

Thus [ends the section]. Here, the word "part" (*ekadeśa*) denotes the locus (*āśrita*), while the word "locus" (*āśraya*) denotes the subject (*pakṣa*). An example is as follows: from seeing smoke on a mountain—where the smoke has a known necessary connection with fire in places such as a kitchen—one gains knowledge of the fire residing on that mountain. But what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding this necessity of connection? It cannot be perception (*pratyakṣa*), because perception is restricted to objects existing in a proximate place and at the present time. Nor can it be mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), because that is not independent regarding external objects. Even [perception] aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of repeated observation is not capable [of establishing it], because the latent impression...

Because [the relation] has mere recollection as its cause. It is said: first, the conjunction of smoke and fire is manifested by perception. That [conjunction], moreover, exists as a qualifier of a substance, because qualities have a nature that is dependent upon a substance. Smoke and fire, however, exist as the qualificands; and space and time also exist solely as qualifiers of the substance, just like the conjunction, but not as qualifiers of the conjunction itself. For instance, the cognition is "these two are conjoined," and not "this is the conjunction of these two. Indeed, the state of being "this" (idantā) consists in existing in a proximate place and at the present time, and that [state] is dependent upon the substance.

Therefore, in this case, first of all, in the kitchen and so forth, the conjunction of fire with smoke is perceived as being indeed unrestricted by space and time. That [conjunction] is thus intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). Consequently, it is understood that the connection of fire with smoke is invariably concomitant with smoke alone. And thus, in another place or at another time, only the existence of smoke requires a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); but once that exists, the conjunction with fire does not, because it has already been known to be invariably concomitant with that [smoke] alone.

Therefore, at the very moment the restriction of the relation is determined, since the connection with fire and so forth is understood through the fact that smoke is invariably concomitant with it, the validity of inference is not untenable—even though it apprehends what has already been apprehended—because it is a direct experience (*anubhūti*), just like a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika*). Thus, the initial perception alone is the means of valid knowledge regarding the restriction of the relation between smoke and fire; subsequently, through repeated observation, its status as being free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhikatva*) is ascertained, because no limiting condition is perceived even when sought with great effort.

Therefore, even repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is purposeful, as it has been respected by the teachers. However, where the conjunction first apprehended is later sometimes obstructed—as in the case of smoke with fire—the limitation of place and time is subsequently introduced; thus, because it lacks inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*), it is considered adventitious (*aupādhika*). And the adventitious condition (*upādhi*) is the connection with wet fuel, since smoke is invariably concomitant with that alone.

Thus, it is established that in other cases as well, wherever a relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is perceived as being without limiting conditions (*nirupādhika*) by whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), in each such instance, that very means of valid cognition is the proof. As it has been said:

"Whatever relationship exists here between one thing and another, when it is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or other means of valid cognition as being without limiting conditions, that [relationship] is held to be the indicator (*gamaka*) of that [other]."

Thus it is said. Regarding this, some who follow the position of the Teacher (Ācārya) say: "Fire and smoke have conjoined, they conjoin, and they will conjoin"—thus, it is understood that the three times delimit the very act of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is the meaning of the verbal root. It is not [the case that the times delimit the substances].

Furthermore, time need not necessarily be indicated by the word "this" (*idam*) alone, since it can be indicated even more clearly by verbal suffixes such as the present tense (*laṭ*). Or, let us grant that there is no comprehension of the conjunction’s delimitation by either space or time; nevertheless, its inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) remains unproven. For the determination of that [inherent nature] is not established merely by the non-comprehension of a delimitation, since it is possible for something that exists to remain uncomprehended. Therefore, as long as the possibility of a delimitation remains undetermined, its inherent nature cannot be proven.

To this it is replied: We maintain that the delimitation by time (*kālāvaccheda*) of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not perceived through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*); however, we do not deny the temporal delimitation of conjunction by way of the verbal suffixes such as the *laṭ* (present tense) established by grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), because that [instruction] is of no use for the perception of pervasion. Indeed, the delimitation by time is useful for its apprehension precisely through the means of valid cognition that grasp it. Nor do we assert that [conjunction] is inherent merely because its temporal delimitation is not cognized, since repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) also serves as an auxiliary factor.

Therefore, when it is determined that [the relation] is without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), its inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) is firmly established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*).

Furthermore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like are in reality dependent in nature upon substance (*dravya*), whereas substance is independent. Consequently, the state of being delimited (*avacchedyatva*) belongs primarily to the substance itself. However, where there is no dispute regarding the possibility [of delimitation], even a factor such as conjunction, acting as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), is delimited by time—as, for example, the connection between fire and smoke. For this very reason, it is said to be adventitious (*aupādhika*).

And that inference is of two kinds, distinguished as being for one's own sake (svārtha) and for the sake of others (parārtha). Inference for one's own sake is the arising of inference through a collection of factors [of evidence] synthesized by oneself; whereas inference for the sake of others is that which is awakened by a statement employed by another.

And that statement consists of three members; these are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*udāharaṇa*). Among these, the proposition is the first to be employed. However, there is no fixed rule regarding the order of employment for the reason and the example. The recollection of the necessary connection (*saṃbandha-niyama*), even when preceded by the perception of one part (*ekadeśa-darśana*), serves as the awakener of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*); likewise, the perception of one part is also [the awakener] when it is preceded by the recollection of the necessary connection.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that since the probandum is established by the employment of either the reason (*hetu*) or the application (*upanaya*), the inclusion of both is redundant. Furthermore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is likewise useless, because the probandum is already obtained through the force of the reason as it has been stated. Similarly, the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is not a constituent part of inference. The capacity of the reason to produce knowledge arises from the necessity of its connection with the property to be proven; and this [necessity] is fully supported by the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) alone—so what is the use [of the other]?

By means of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). For this very reason, even a statement of a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-udāharaṇa*) employed by some there with the intent of establishing [the point] is entirely useless. If it is argued that there would then be an option (*vikalpa*), we say no, because the means are not equal; for one is straightforward while the other is circuitous. An option occurs only between two things of an equal nature. For this very reason, certain Mīmāṃsakas do not accept purely negative inference (*kevala-vyatireki-anumāna*), because the relationship between the probandum and the probans is well-established in a similar instance (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*), and such an instance is absent here.

The distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), however, should be understood as it is in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*). When, by the etymological derivation "inference is that by which one infers" (*anumīyate 'neneti anumānam*), the knowledge of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the means of valid cognition, then the subsequent cognition of avoidance (*hāna*) and so forth is the result. But when, by the derivation "inference is that by which one infers" (*anumīyate 'neneti anumānam*), the term refers to the instrument (*karaṇa*), then cognitions and the like do not constitute the instrument, since the status of being an instrument is merely relative to the speaker's intention. In all cases, the result is simply the cognition whose object is the inferential mark (*liṅga*).

In this regard, we shall explain the validity of worldly statements through the form of inference on the occasion of discussing verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*). Therefore, all of this has been described extensively in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, within the section on inference (*anumāna-pariccheda*) in the *Pramāṇapārāyaṇa*. Since our work is concerned solely with the tenets established within our own specific system (*pratitantra-siddhānta*), we have no mandate for further elaboration.
Now, the simile.

Comparison (*upamāna*) is the cognition of similarity residing in another object similar to a given one, arising from the perception of that [given] object. For example, when a person who has previously seen a cow sees a *gavaya* (wild ox) in the forest that is similar to it, the cognition of the similarity residing in the cow—which has the *gavaya* as its counter-correlative—namely, "My cow is similar to this," is comparison. This is not perception, because it arises with respect to a cow that is beyond the range of sensory contact (*cakṣussannikarṣa*). Nor is it memory, because there was no prior experience of such [a cow] at that time, and memory is preceded by such experience.

However, the cognition of the cow is merely memory (*smṛti*). Nor is it inference (*anumāna*), because it lacks the prerequisite of a prior apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and its recollection. By the phrase "from the perception of similarity," the status of sensory cognition of similarity as *upamāna* is refuted. As for the remaining part [of the definition], the fact that the cognition of the commonality of many parts—which follows from the perception of similarity—and the similarity itself are distinct categories will be established on the occasion of defining the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
Now, presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

When there is no assumption of another meaning, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) operates in a case where one renders another meaning impossible. For example, in the case of "Devadatta is alive, yet he is not in the house," when his absence from the house is seen or heard, the assumption of his being outside occurs because, in the absence of that [external presence], his absence from the house makes his being alive impossible; thus, it postulates his being outside. And here, "impossibility" (*anupapatti*) means doubt.

For instance: when the external existence [of the person] and his absence from the house have not been conceptualized, there remains only doubt as to whether he is alive or not. But once that has been conceptualized, the doubt subsides. That which brings about doubt regarding an object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The conceptualization of external existence is the valid cognition (*pramā*). The object being conceptualized is the object of cognition (*prameya*). Alternatively, according to the etymological derivation that "valid cognition is the instrument of right knowledge" (*pramiti*), the conceptualization itself is the means of valid cognition; the resulting specific knowledge that follows immediately thereafter is the fruit (*phala*).

Is it not the case that the postulation of Devadatta’s existence outside based on the observation of his absence from the house is indeed inference? For instance: "Devadatta exists outside, because while being alive, he is not present in the house; for whoever is alive and is not in a certain place exists elsewhere, just as I am. If this is argued, we say: not so, because there is doubt regarding the element of his being alive.

[Objection: But how can life, which is known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), be considered doubtful? [Reply: True; for when an object has been cognized, doubt certainly arises if it acquires a form different from the form previously apprehended. Previously, life was cognized as being connected exclusively with the house. Now, that connection having ceased and no connection with an external location having been established, doubt regarding life certainly arises. "Previously, while living, Devadatta was seen only in the house."

"Now he is not at home, or perhaps he does not even live. If it is argued that "in that case, because of the postulation of a connection with an external location, his being alive is an unambiguous mark (*liṅga*)," [we reply: there would be an absence of an object to be inferred (*anumeya*). It is precisely the connection with an external location that is desired to be inferred. If that [connection] were already determined, nothing would remain to be inferred. Furthermore, mere absence from the house is not a valid mark, as it deviates in the cases of one who is dead or one yet to be born. Therefore, there is no room for inference here. Consequently, it is established that presumption (*arthāpatti*) is a matter that gives rise to doubt.

For smoke and the like are not the mark (*liṅga*) of any object by way of producing doubt; therefore, there is a difference [between presumption and inference]. Likewise, in the case of "The fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," fatness is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for nocturnal eating, provided that nocturnal eating has not yet been imagined. As it has been said: "That conceptual construction which proceeds in order to eliminate a doubt regarding an object is known as presumption (*arthāpatti*), because it arises from an object that was the source of the doubt."

Thus [it was said]. Others, however, held this view: when an object, even though perceived, undergoes a transformation of its previously observed nature such that it incurs an inconsistency in the form of doubt, that object serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of another object in order to dispel the doubt regarding itself. For example, the aforementioned general fact of being alive and the mere act of eating. Inference from smoke and the like is not of this kind; there is a difference because in one case the cause is uncertain, while in the other it is doubted. As it has been said:
"When an object, even though perceived, falls into doubt without the postulation [of something else]..."
Therefore, some declare that very conceptualization to be presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

Thus [it is said]. However, some say that the very absence from the house, being otherwise inexplicable, serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of his being outside. That is incorrect. In that case, what is the inexplicability of the absence from the house? If you say it is that "his own absence [from the house] would not occur if he were not present outside," then this is merely the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which is the absence of the reason when the probandum is absent.

And since that [absence] is understood through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), characterized by the presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) when the reason (*hetu*) is present, this is indeed inference (*anumāna*) because it operates by way of both positive and negative concomitance; thus, there is no possibility for *arthāpatti* to have a separate status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it is established that *arthāpatti* is either the object that gives rise to doubt, or the object in which doubt has been induced by that [reason].

On this point, some say: where the non-occurrence of a fact is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there another fact must be postulated; this is *dṛṣṭārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is seen). However, where [the non-occurrence] is established by a sentence—as in "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day"—there the sentence itself, "He eats at night," must be postulated, according to the maxim: "A verbal expectancy is fulfilled only by a word. Therefore, they claim that there is a twofold division of presumption: *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard). That is incorrect.

In this case as well, it is more appropriate to postulate the meaning itself; for when that [meaning] is not postulated there is an inconsistency, whereas when it is postulated, that inconsistency is resolved. Therefore, that alone should be postulated. Otherwise, if one were to postulate the word or sentence itself—on the grounds that the inconsistency is resolved by the use of words and sentences whose meanings are unknown—then one would have to postulate those very words and sentences. In that case, since the resolution of the inconsistency follows simply from the knowledge of the word-meanings, it is the postulation of the meaning alone that is stated to be necessary. Furthermore, to postulate both would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Since it is observed that in the case of presumption based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*), it is the object itself that is to be postulated, let that very thing be postulated here as well. For verbal expectancy (*śābdī ākāṅkṣā*) is satisfied even by the connection with a postulated object, because that alone is what is expected. For this very reason, in cases of ellipsis such as "The door," the denotation is connected with the mental [object] of closing and so forth, and not with the supplied word "Let it be closed," since denotation through connection is possible even with an object present in the mind, though not expressed by a word. Furthermore, the use of a word toward another may occur in some instances due to the force of a desire to know (*jijñāsā*), but it is not a rule.

[Objection: Presumption (*arthāpatti*) proceeds for the sake of postulating an object, because that object is the domain of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), and since these cognitions are preceded by words, presumption operates as far as the word denoting that object. [Reply: This is not so, because this [dependence on words] is absent in all cases of determinate perception and in inference based on one's own [experience]. Indeed, those two do not operate as far as the word; for it is impossible for them to do so in the case of the deaf, the mute, or animals. Rather, they operate toward the mere object itself.

Furthermore, in all conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), that which appears is the mental representation resulting from the hearing of a word, and not the object of knowledge itself. To claim that "the expressive word is remembered because of the perception of the object" is untenable to critical inquiry. We shall, however, examine the word as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in its proper place. Therefore, including presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), there are five means of valid cognition. All of this has been elaborated upon in the *Pramāṇapārāyaṇa*; since it is not useful for the investigation of the meaning of the Vedas, we have no great insistence on it here.
Refutation of Non-existence as a Means of Valid Cognition (Abhāvapramāṇanirāsa)

Some accept a sixth means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), called non-existence (abhāva), for the apprehension of non-existence. They argue that since non-existence is distinct from existence, it cannot be grasped by the means of valid cognition whose nature is existence; therefore, a means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence must be sought, characterized by the non-arising of the five [other] means of valid cognition. This is incorrect, because there is no object of knowledge (prameya) [for such a means]. But how can there be its absence? For there is indeed the cognition: "There is no jar here on this ground."

Does that [cognition] have as its object the nature of the ground together with [the absence], or does it have only that [absence] as its object? Not the first, because it would then follow [erroneously] even in the case of a place where a jar is present. Nor the second, because it does not escape the previously mentioned defects. In the second case, however, one must admit the existence of absence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, regarding the ground and so forth which are devoid of thorns and the like, is the practice of walking about without hesitation based on the determination of the ground alone, or is it the determination of the bare ground?

Furthermore, in that case, there would be unhesitating practical activity even regarding subtle thorns and the like, even when they have not been cognized; and the desire to know them, which is preceded by effort, would be rendered superfluous. In the second case, however, an object of knowledge called "absence" (abhāva) would have to be admitted; for only then would practical activity based on the determination of that [absence] be logical, as well as the desire to know it for the sake of reflecting upon its counter-positive (pratiyogin). Moreover, if absence were not admitted, the word "is not" (nāsti) would be devoid of meaning.

There would be an inference of horns for rabbits and the like, and there would be no sublation (bādha) of the cognition "this is silver. However, if that [sublation] is accepted, it becomes meaningful; and it is logical that the object of an inference should be subject to sublation. Sublation, moreover, is logical. Therefore, there exists another reality (tattvāntara) distinct from existence (bhāva).

Now we shall investigate this: is that [absence] to be understood through the means of valid cognition for existence (*bhāva-pramāṇa*), or is it to be understood through the cognition of non-existence (*abhāva*)? In this regard, it cannot first be understood through perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is cognized even when the operation of the sense organs has ceased. How is this determined? Non-existence must be apprehended somewhere as "something is not here. Consequently, the sense organ ceases its activity precisely at the apprehension of that [locus] where [the absence] is to be apprehended; it does not operate toward the apprehension of the non-existence itself, because there is no connection between the two.

Therefore, non-existence is the object of the means of knowledge known as non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*). How is this distinction determined? It is said: having experienced the nature of a house or the like, a person who has gone to another place, when questioned regarding the absence of another object, receives the answer "it is not there" from the questioner who desires to know that other entity. As it has been stated: "The observer perceives only the intrinsic nature [of the place], and later, even while recollecting something [else], when asked about its non-existence therein, he understands it exactly so."

Thus [it is argued]. Furthermore, there is no operation of the sense organ in that case, because of the spatial distance. Therefore, the cognition of absence is not sensory (aindriyikī). Consequently, it cannot be said that absence is perceptible (pratyakṣa). Nor can it be said that the absence was first apprehended and subsequently exists in the intellect (buddhistha), because at that time the counter-positive (pratiyogin) has not yet entered the intellect. Nor should it be asserted that what was previously experienced by indeterminate perception (nirvikalpaka) is later remembered by determinate perception (savikalpaka).

Because an absence whose form is necessarily commensurate with its counter-positive is always beyond the scope of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*); or, if such [an indeterminate cognition] were possible, even the memory would be of that same nature, since memory conforms to the original experience.

Nor is there inference, because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*); for here no mark pervaded by non-existence (*abhāva*) is perceived. There is likewise no occasion for presumption based on what is possible (*upapatti*) or presumption based on what is otherwise inexplicable (*arthāpatti*). Therefore, in each case, it is simply the non-arising of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a positive entity that serves as the means of valid cognition for the apprehension of non-existence.

Objection: Might the non-arising of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇānutpatti*) serve as a means of valid cognition by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*)? No; because both [the absence of the mark and the absence of the probandum] are of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvātmaka*), it is impossible to grasp their pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a means of valid cognition that apprehends positive entities (*bhāva*). Therefore, the means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (*abhāva*) presents its own object solely through its own inherent power.

However, some say that in cases where there is the absence of a perceptible object, non-apprehension of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); but in other cases, either a positive or a negative means of valid cognition would apply as appropriate. Therefore, because the object of knowledge (*prameya*) exists, the means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (*abhāva*) must be accepted.

To this it is replied: there are two kinds of cognition regarding the ground and so forth; one has a composite object, while the other has that [ground] alone as its object. That latter kind is also twofold: when the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is invisible and when it is visible. Among these, the cognition that has that [ground] alone as its object when the counter-positive is visible is itself called the non-existence (*abhāva*) of that counter-positive. Non-existence is not merely the cognition having that alone as its object, for that would lack specificity; rather, it is [that cognition] when the counter-positive is visible.

Consequently, when a counter-positive (pratiyogin) is perceptible, that cognition which has exclusively that [counter-positive] as its object is designated as its absence; thus, when it is said, "There is no jar on this ground," it is meant that the bare ground was not perceived while the jar was perceptible.

Now, what indeed is this so-called "perceptibility" (*dṛśyatva*) in the case of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)? According to your own established position, it is the occurrence of something already cognized elsewhere in another location; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of negating what has not been mentally presented (*aprasakta-pratiṣedha*). Let that very thing be "perceptibility. For us, however, it is a specific kind of cognition. Even for one who accepts a distinct category called "non-existence" (*abhāva*), the cognition of non-existence is desired only by accepting a cognition whose object is that [locus] alone, following the cognition of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). This is because the mental presentation of the counter-positive is the cause of that [cognition of non-existence].

In this regard, it must be considered what kind of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is perceived as the cause [of the cognition of absence]: is it one accompanied by another, or one qualified by the absence [of the counter-positive], or one that is independent and solitary? Not the first, because if the locus were perceived even when conjoined with a jar, there would follow the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving the absence of that jar. Not the second, because it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

For, having first cognized the locus as qualified by that [absence] based upon the absence itself, one subsequently apprehends that very absence; thus, the cognition of the absence is itself the cause for the comprehension of the absence. Therefore, even when the absence is not [separately] perceived, the perception of the mere nature of the locus must be admitted. Consequently, the third position remains: since the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding absence is established by that much alone, what is the purpose of postulating an additional distinct category (*tattvāntara*)? Such a distinct category is not perceived, unlike [colors such as] blue or yellow. [It might be argued: "The atoms of air possess a blue color..."

In such cases as "the atoms of water are devoid of odor," there is a cognition consisting of inference whose sole object is that [absence]. The point is this: among the four kinds of absences, for whichever absence there is a locus in your view where the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is perceptible, for us, the cognition having that very locus as its object is itself the absence. Furthermore, the word "does not exist" denotes only such a locus, and the negative particle (*nañ*) refers merely to the essential nature [of the locus], according to the Prābhākaras.

Even everyday activities such as walking with confidence are caused solely by a cognition whose object is that [single entity]. Even the desire to know (jijñāsā) is appropriate for the sake of attaining perceptibility. Likewise, sublation by perception and sublation by inference are caused either solely by a cognition whose object is that [single entity] or solely by the sublation of the activity. The Prābhākaras maintain that it is the activity regarding mother-of-pearl as silver, or the activity regarding a pseudo-inferential mark as a valid mark, that is sublated; for it is not the cognition that is sublated, but rather the activity alone.

Now, if there is no other such thing as non-existence (*abhāva*), then how does a cognition having that [jar] as its sole object arise in a place where previously there was a cognition of its connection [with the ground]? Or, according to your own view, how is there the apprehension of non-existence there? If you say it is due to the impact of a mallet or similar causes, then for us as well, a cognition having that as its sole object is produced by those very same causes. By this, the claim that the continued existence of a jar brought to another location is the cause of the cognition having that as its sole object is also explained away.

Now, if there is no other entity called "non-existence" (abhāva), then when a series of potsherds is produced by the striking of a mallet or similar means, why would the cognition that previously had that [jar] as its sole object not subsequently also have a conjoined object as its domain? Or, according to your view, why should it not be so? If you say it is because of the destruction of the positive entity (bhāva) itself, then the same would apply to us as well. If you then argue that this implies the acceptance of non-existence, we too accept destruction, but not as the arising of another positive entity.

Existence itself, however, attains two states: being alone and being accompanied by another. Among these, existence in its solitary state is precisely what is denoted by the term "destruction. It has been stated previously that even in your own view, such a state must necessarily be admitted. Thus, even in the case of things like cognitions which perish without leaving a trace (niranvaya-vināśin), the persistence of the substratum's own nature should be understood as the arising of another existence.

Furthermore, even for one who maintains that there is another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the non-arising of a cognition characterized by non-apprehension does not indicate the absence of an object by virtue of its own existence, because it would follow that all things are cognized as absent during states such as sleep. Moreover, consider an object that was previously unseen in a certain place and is later seen again in that very same place.

The absence that is simultaneous with the perception is determined by the thought, "This was not here previously. Consequently, since the absence of perception has ceased due to that [present] perception, it must be stated that it is precisely the prior absence of perception, when being recollected, that is the cause of the cognition of absence. And thus, it must be admitted that only a known non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the cause of the cognition of absence. Furthermore, since non-apprehension itself is of the nature of an absence, its own manifestation would likewise be unapprehended, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If the cognition has that [self] as its sole object, it does not depend on another means of knowledge because it is self-luminous (*svayaṃ-prakāśatayā*). Therefore, there is no non-inclusion of a means of knowledge; rather, by its power, the object of knowledge is established. Thus, it is proven that there are exactly five means of knowledge.
