We shall discuss verbal testimony (*śābda*) at its proper occasion. All of this has been established by Śālikānātha in the *Amṛtakalā*.
Thus ends the first chapter, on the Means of Valid Cognition (*pramāṇa*), in the *Tantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Rāmānuja.
Now begins the chapter on the objects of cognition.
Now, the category of the objects of cognition (prameya) is defined.

In this regard, by the principle of a tenet accepted for the sake of argument (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*), the very category of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) established in the system of Kaṇāda is accepted, because this work is undertaken for the purpose of expounding that system. However, it is not explained here separately; rather, within that system, portions that are undesirable are refuted, while the specific portions are explained.

Thus, there are eight categories (*padārtha*): substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), inherence (*samavāya*), power (*śakti*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and similarity (*sādṛśya*).
In that regard, the substances are nine: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind.

In this regard, air is indeed directly perceived; however, it is not merely its tactile quality that is perceived, for even when there is a difference between cold and hot touch, there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is the same air. Now, one might object: "Air has a tactile quality that is neither hot nor cold; how can it be recognized when that [quality] differs? This is not a valid objection, as the case is comparable to that of rock crystal (*sphaṭika*). For just as a white rock crystal, despite being connected to various adventitious qualities, is recognized in its substrate through such cognitions as "that which was white is this very same red one," so too is the case here.

In this regard, it is earth alone that initiates the body, and not the other elements, because they are not perceived [as such]; furthermore, this is observed in the continuous succession of contemporary women and men. The opposite view is simply non-existent. And that [body] is of three kinds only, distinguished as viviparous, oviparous, and sweat-born. As for plants and the like, which are "sprout-born," they are not bodies because no experience of pleasure or pain is perceived; for that [experience] is the purpose for which the body serves as a locus. As it is said: "In the cremation ground grows a tree frequented by herons and vultures."
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a person goes to the state of being stationary.

This statement is not independent, as it is dependent upon a specific injunction; for it contradicts valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), just like [the statements] "The sacrificer is the animal" or "The sacrificial post is the sun."

Likewise, the self is not an object of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), because there is a contradiction between the status of being an object and that of being an agent. The designation "I know myself" is merely figurative. Rather, while objects are being manifested, the self shines forth as the substratum of cognition. Every instance of consciousness manifests a triad; necessarily, the experience of the knower persists within the experiences of the objects of knowledge. Otherwise, there would be no distinction between what is cognized by oneself and what is cognized by another. And it is only when this is so that the rule of the necessary concomitant apprehension with the objects is logically established.

For the self does not appear as something that conforms to objects, nor do objects appear while the cognizer remains unmanifest. Therefore, consciousness itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object; it is that very consciousness which makes the person (*puruṣa*) its object. Thus, even though the person partakes in the fruit of that consciousness, he does not possess the status of an object (*karman*), but rather the status of an agent (*kartṛ*). Those who know the nature of action define an object as "that which possesses the fruit of an action inherent in another [the agent]. Consequently, [the self] is not perceived by mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).

Darkness is not a distinct substance; it is merely the misconception of blueness, as in the case of those who are blind. Shadow is simply a portion of the ground or other such objects from which light has been excluded.

The qualities (guṇas), however, are color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, momentum, sound, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, and merit.

The distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal among these, as well as the manner of their origination, subsistence, and destruction, is established in the system of Kaṇāda; however, since these are not useful for the investigation of the meaning of the Vedas, we have no concern with them.

Action (*karman*), however, is always to be inferred; for motion is inferred through a succession of conjunctions and disjunctions. The inference of the sun’s motion from its arrival at different locations is elaborated upon in the *Bhāṣya*. This very action is directly enjoined by virtue of being something to be accomplished in itself (*svataḥ-sādhyatayā*). In the case of substance and quality, which are established entities by nature, [action is enjoined] through their connection with that [action]. For instance, in the injunction "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), curd is enjoined precisely as being colored by the oblation; likewise, in "one purchases with a red [cow]," the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) is also [enjoined].

Jāti (universal) exists only in perceptible substances and nowhere else, because it is not perceived elsewhere. Its cognition occurs as follows: in perceptible substances such as jars and cloths, it is grasped through the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) by the sense organs that grasp their respective substrates; thus, while existing as a single form across various individuals, it is entirely distinct from them. At the apprehension of the first individual, it is cognized merely in its own essential nature; however, at the apprehensions of the second and subsequent individuals, it is recognized as "this is that very same [universal]" through the recollection of the previous form.
Being recognized, it manifests without distinction between the common person and the investigator. As it has been said:
"The universal (jāti), though distinct from its substratum, is the object of perceptual cognition;
according to the teacher Prabhākara, it is [grasped] through the recollection of a previous form."

Thus [it is said]: for a genus (*jāti*) is indeed persistent (*anuvṛtta*), and persistence is its property. Therefore, at the time of perceiving the first individual (*piṇḍa*), because there is no recollection of other individuals, that persistence is not perceived. However, in the perceptions of the second and subsequent individuals, it is perceived because such recollection is possible. For where a person determines a difference yet simultaneously possesses a cognition of non-difference, a genus is postulated there due to this logical necessity (*anupapatti*). And the recognition of the genus (*jāti-pratyabhijñā*) occurs precisely in that case.

For this very reason, among the many flames occurring within a single wick that are subject to destruction in each moment, "flame-ness" (*jvālātva*) is not the object of recognition. This is because, as in the case of silver perceived in a mother-of-pearl shell, there is no perception of a difference between individuals due to the non-apprehension of their distinction. Some, however, have maintained that the universal (*jāti*) is both different and non-different from the individuals; that is untenable, because it involves a contradiction. Nor can this contradiction be resolved by the force of perception, since such perception itself is impossible.

For ordinary people hold that an object is distinct when it is cognized by a distinct cognition, and non-distinct when it is cognized by a non-distinct cognition. In that case, at the time of perceiving two things, the universal (*jāti*) would have to be perceived as either distinct from or non-distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), and likewise the individual would have to be perceived as such in relation to the universal; consequently, there would be a double appearance. But this is not observed. Therefore, there is indeed a difference between the two. Even though that difference exists, there is no such cognition here as "the cowness is here in the cow," in the same way as one says "the jujube fruit is here in the bowl.
For every form (*rūpa*) is never perceived apart from that which possesses the form (*rūpin*). Therefore...

Since a universal (jāti) is perceived by the same sense organ as the individual (vyakti), it enters into the cognition of the individual; however, since an action (karman) is inferred, it does not enter into the cognition of the individual, and thus the cognition [of the action] occurs here quite independently.

Some, however, claim that there is a universal called "existence" (sattā) because the cognition "existent, existent" recurs with respect to the triad of substance and so forth; that is incorrect. For one who gazes without blinking at various heterogeneous things—such as mustard seeds and mountains, or at colors and so forth, or at actions—a cognition of "existence" that conforms to a prior form does not arise. As for the recurrence of usage, it is based solely on an adventitious condition (upādhi), just like words such as "cook. And this adventitious condition is simply the fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Furthermore, your own admission that the application of the word "existent" (*sat*) in the triad of qualities is based solely on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) would apply in all cases alike. By this very logic, substance-ness (*dravyatva*), earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), sound-ness (*śabdatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth—which reside in perceptible and imperceptible things—are also refuted, because no corresponding recurring form (*anugatākāra*) manifests [to the mind]. The persistence of these linguistic applications is merely due to limiting adjuncts; and those adjuncts are simply the respective definitions (*lakṣaṇa*). Moreover, you yourself have accepted that these very definitions serve as the manifestors (*vyañjaka*) of universals (*jāti*).

If it is argued that universals such as cowness, existence, and substantiality do not flash forth instantly and universally for everyone, but rather only for those whose intellects have been trained by means of scripture upon the investigation of their manifestors—alas, this is a denial of the mental experience of all people, namely, that a single entity is perceived through an unstable mode of apprehension. Furthermore, by this same logic, even cowness would not be established, because one could not exclude those who disagree [on its definition] regarding an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth. By this very reasoning, Brahminhood, Kshatriyahood, and so on, are likewise untenable.

If it is argued that, in that case, the scriptures would not function according to the established distinctions between those respective castes (*varṇa*), we say: not so. Within the beginningless stream of *saṃsāra*, there exist certain male and female individuals—established by worldly consensus—who are denoted by terms such as "Brahmin" and so forth, and who are not "first-time" instances (i.e., they have no beginning). Brahminhood and the other castes consist precisely in being descended from them. And the scripture has only that [descent] as its object. Furthermore, since you yourself have accepted that [scripture] functions as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) [of caste], nothing is untenable. All of this has been explained in detail in the section titled "The Determination of Caste" (*Jātinirṇaya*).

The Vaiśeṣikas, however, assert that in eternal substances which possess identical qualities, actions, and genera, there exists a property called "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) which serves as the cause for their mutual differentiation. This is untenable, because differentiation is established by "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) alone. If it is argued that since separateness is common to all substances, it cannot establish absolute differentiation among eternal substances, we say: not so; for that [separateness] is simply impossible in them. If it is argued that its possibility exists for those who perceive it, we reply: no, because such perceivers do not exist. For that which is unfit [for perception] cannot be perceived.

The real entity (*vastu*) is directly perceived. If it is argued that atoms must be perceptible to someone because they are objects of cognition (*meyatva*), like a jar, and thus their existence is established—[we reply: this is not so, because external perceptibility is unestablished due to their being partless substances (*niravayavadravyatva*), and mental perceptibility is unestablished due to their being corporeal (*mūrtatva*). Therefore, the particularities (*viśeṣas*) remain as the subject of debate.

Inherence (*samavāya*) is the relationship between two things that are not established as separate. It is eternal when it pertains to two eternal things; it is non-eternal when it pertains to two non-eternal things, or to one eternal and one non-eternal thing. Its origination occurs from the very same source from which its effect originates. Furthermore, it is always inferable, because it is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

In all entities, a supersensible power (*śakti*) is inferred from its effect. For instance: although burning is observed to occur only from fire as it naturally is, when gems, mantras, or medicinal herbs are employed, burning is not observed from fire in that same state. Therefore, there must exist something supersensible—denotable by such terms as "power" (*śakti*), "capacity" (*sāmarthya*), and so forth—which is either obstructed by the gems, mantras, and the like, or destroyed by them. Furthermore, the production of this [power] arises from the causes of its own substratum.

When an effect does not arise, there are two possibilities: either suppression (*abhibhava*) or destruction (*vināśa*). Where an effect is not produced, there is destruction; however, where it is produced, there is suppression. [Objection: But surely the non-arising of the effect would occur simply due to the proximity of gems, mantras, and so forth. [Response: No, because as long as the causal factors are unimpaired, the obstruction of the arising of the effect is impossible. [Objection: In that case, the non-application of those [gems and mantras] must also be a cause for its production. [Response: No.

Since the application [of an effort] acts as an obstacle, its absence is merely the cessation of that obstacle; it does not, however, possess the status of a causal factor (*nimitta*). Rather, the production of the effect arises solely from the capacity (*śakti*) whose obstacles have been removed. Furthermore, since we observe the production of an effect even when there has been some application [of effort], provided there is a remedy, the absence of that application cannot be the causal factor.

Even if one accepts that [gravity] is a cause (*nimitta*), if its causal capacity (*śakti*) is denied, then gravity would be rendered as good as dead; for when the fall is obstructed by contact with a tangible substance, it is precisely the absence of that [obstruction] which serves as the cause of the fall. For such is the established position of your own doctrine: that in the absence of an obstruction, falling occurs due to gravity.

As it has been said: "In the absence of conjunction and effort, falling occurs due to gravity. This is because even when those [conjunction and effort] are present, the effect is not produced; for whatever does not produce an effect despite the presence of something else must depend on something additional to that, just as a seed alone [does not produce a sprout]. Furthermore, if potentiality (*śakti*) were not admitted, there would be no reason for seekers of an effect to employ specific causes. But if it is admitted, then the rule is established that only that which is capable is employed, and nothing else.

Likewise, number (*saṃkhyā*) is also a distinct category (*tattvāntara*). To explain: it is not a substance (*dravya*), because it subsists in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—as in the expressions "smell is twofold" or "touch is threefold. If it is argued that its subsistence there is merely figurative (*aupacārikī*), we say no; for there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against its primary sense. If it is argued that its very nature as a quality (*guṇatva*) is the subverting evidence, we say no; for that [nature] is unestablished. It is not a quality, because it subsists in many things, like "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and the like. It is not action (*karma*), because it is perceptible and because its cognition differs from that of action. It is not a universal (*sāmānya*), because it is non-eternal. Therefore, it is a distinct category.

Likewise, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is not a substance (*dravya*), because it subsists even in qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*). For odors and so forth appear to be mutually similar: an odor [is similar] to another odor, and likewise a color, and likewise an action. For this very reason, it is neither a quality nor an action. Nor is it a universal (*sāmānya*), because it lacks the character of being the cause for a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*). If it is argued that similarity is a "universal consisting of a plurality of common parts" (*bhūyo'vayavasāmānya*), we say no, because of the difference in the nature of the cognition [involved].

For similarity is perceived only as having a counter-correlate (sapratyogika), in the form "this is similar to that. Moreover, it is that [counter-correlate] which manifests it, since the perception of similarity occurs only with respect to that. Therefore, it is a distinct category (tattvāntara).

The entire range of objects of knowledge is subsumed within five sheaths: the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), the locus of enjoyment (*bhogāyatana*), the instruments of enjoyment (*bhogasādhana*), the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*), and the act of enjoyment (*bhukti*). The self (*ātman*) is the enjoyer; the body is the locus of enjoyment; the sense organs are the instruments of enjoyment; the objects of enjoyment are of two kinds—internal and external; the external ones are earth and so forth, while the internal ones are pleasure and so forth; and enjoyment is the experience of pleasure and pain.

Liberation (*mokṣa*) is also a distinct human goal (*puruṣārtha*), characterized by the total eradication of all suffering. Its attainment, however, results from the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) as enjoined by such scriptural passages as, "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon," and "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. One who has turned away from various perishable human goals and desires the destruction of all suffering is the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*) for this; others, however, are qualified for ritual action (*karma*).

All treatises on ritual action (*karmaśāstra*) proceed with reference to that [person] alone, whereas treatises on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*) concern the person other than that; thus, the thorough knowledge of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is purposeful in both ways.
Thus ends the second chapter, on the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), in the *Tantrarahasya* composed by the venerable teacher Rāmānuja.
Verbal Authority (Śābdapramāṇa)

Thus have the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and the resulting cognitions (*miti*) been described. Now, verbal testimony (*śabda*) as a means of knowledge is being examined. A collection of words that conveys an object by virtue of grasping a [conventional] relationship is verbal testimony. That very same [collection of words], when its object is not in contact with the senses, is scripture (*śāstra*).
As it has been said: "Scripture is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] arising from the cognition of words."

Thus: verbal testimony (*śāstra*) is that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which consists of a cognition whose object is an unperceived thing, arising from the contact of the self and the mind dependent upon the knowledge of words. On the other hand, worldly speech has as its object things perceived through other means of valid cognition; it is therefore of the nature of inference (*anumāna*), and thus not *śāstra*. That it is of the nature of inference will be explained later. First, the relationship between word and meaning is characterized by the state of signifier and signified—that is to say, the relationship of denoter and denoted—and this is non-human (*apauruṣeya*) in origin. As it has been said:

"But the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate; the knowledge thereof is instruction, which is non-deviant regarding an unperceived object; that is a means of valid cognition according to Bādarāyaṇa, because of its independence. "Innate" (autpattika) means natural, not human-made, and eternal. Because phonemes are eternal and meanings are eternal by way of their continuity, the relationship is not human-made.

Now, how can phonemes (*varṇa*) be eternal? They are heard as having their completion solely in their utterance. For instance, this much is beyond dispute: impelled by human effort with respect to the utterance of various phonemes, the internal air rising from the region of the navel-center joins with the regions of the chest, throat, head, root of the tongue, teeth, nose, and lips; subsequently, it joins with the region of the listener’s ear, and thereupon the stagnant air located therein departs.

And immediately thereafter, the phonemes (varṇas) are perceived. Likewise, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is simply space (*ākāśa*) delimited by the ear-cavity; sound is its quality, and it is apprehended through inherence (*samavāya*) with that [organ]. Now, this is being investigated: is effort (*prayatna*) productive [of sound], or is it manifesting? It cannot be manifesting, for nothing is manifested either by the removal of an obstruction, or by the refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*), or by the refinement of the object (*viṣaya-saṃskāra*). For there is no such obstruction as a wall or the like between the auditory organ and the sound.

That is possible, because its inherence persists as long as the related entities exist. Furthermore, is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ the nourishment of it by the internal air (*kauṣṭhya-vāyu*), or merely its conjunction with that air? Both of these are compatible even with the theory of production (*utpatti-pakṣa*), since sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa-dharma*) and space itself is the auditory organ (*śrotra*). As for the refinement of the object, that too would have to be a property of the object; however, that is not possible, for there is no connection between the internal air and a property of space.

Even if it were somehow possible [for sound to be produced], this would still be common to the position that sound is produced (*utpattipakṣa*), because even a mediate relationship is observed to be productive. Furthermore, if effort were a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*), it would follow that all sounds would be manifested by a single effort; for there is a rule that things perceptible by the same sense organ do not depend on different manifestors. Indeed, jars and other objects manifested by lamps and the like do not require a multiplicity of those [manifestors]. Moreover, if effort were a manifestor, there would be no conformity to its degrees of intensity; that is, when the effort is weak, [the sound] would be weak, and when intense, intense.

For no variation in the manifestation of a sound is observed to correspond to the variation in intensity of the lamp or other illuminators; furthermore, a single letter such as *ka* is seen to appear as many due to the difference between various speakers, and this is logical only under the theory of production (*utpatti-pakṣa*). Under the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti-pakṣa*), the conventional usage "the sound is eastern" or "the sound is western" would not be possible. However, under the theory of production, it would occur by virtue of the location of the producer; therefore, the formal argument is as follows: sound is non-eternal, because it follows immediately upon an effort that is not a manifestor [of a pre-existing entity], like a jar.

Therefore, sound produced by the conjunction of specific efforts with the respective locations such as the palate and so forth, initiates another sound through a process of successive origination, which then produces the audible sound at the location of the ear. It has been stated that this [final sound] is heard because of its inherence in the auditory organ.

To this it is replied: In all cases regarding words consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*), there is observed the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very same letter *ga*, this is that very same word. This [recognition] is not based on the non-apprehension of difference due to similarity, because no sublation such as "this is not [that]" is observed. In the case of the recognition of a flame, however, difference is established because its causes are known to be distinct. For instance, a flame is first of all a composite substance (*avayavidravya*), and its radiance (*prabhā*) pervades the interior of a house.

For indeed, the diffusion of light is not possible without the dispersal of the flame first ignited; therefore, while the first [flame] has perished and the second is of a different kind, the perception of it there is based on similarity, whereas here, even by way of reasoning, no such sublation is observed. Consequently, when that perception occurs without confusion, it is logical that the effort directed toward each respective phoneme is itself the manifestor.

Furthermore, the opponent's inference is characterized by an unestablished qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*). For the embellishment (*saṃskāra*) is simply the conjunction of the abdominal air with the region of the ear; the removal of the stagnant air is either an invariable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) of that process or its auxiliary cause (*sahakārī*).

Consequently, the auditory organ, being thus refined, perceives the sound; and because air possesses motion, the perception of sound ceases when that conjunction ends. Furthermore, since there is a distinct manifester for each letter, there is no possibility of perceiving all sounds simultaneously. Even on the theory of production (*utpatti-pakṣa*), a distinction among causal factors is indeed admitted; that very distinction is what we call the distinction among manifesters. Therefore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: sound is manifested by effort, because it is perceived immediately after [that effort], provided that it is not produced by it. Whoever...

That which is perceived immediately after something else, while being itself unproduced, is manifested by that [other thing], just as a jar perceived immediately after a lamp is manifested by it. Nor is the qualifying condition here unestablished, because the status of being a manifestor is established by the very fact of its being perceived [immediately after]. Furthermore, there is this reasoning: if phonemes were manifested by effort, they would not depend on differences in effort; for there is a rule that those things perceptible by the same sense organ do not depend on differences in effort, yet such a difference is indeed required.

Therefore, the claim that those [qualities] cannot be manifested by it is likewise one whose foundation is weak; for we observe that among white, blue, and other forms, which are apprehended by the same sense organ, some are manifested by a clear light while others are manifested by a dim light. Similarly, the sweetness of sugar is manifested by only a small amount of saliva, whereas that of parched grain flour and flattened rice requires more than a small amount; likewise, the fragrance of saffron is manifested only by cow's ghee, while the fragrance of musta-grass is manifested by oil, and the fragrance of the earth scorched during the summer season is manifested only by water.

Even the gradations of intensity, such as sharpness or dullness, are consistent with effort being the manifestor; for just as there is a gradation in the perception of color due to the gradation in the light of a lamp, so too is the perception of a single phoneme as having various forms due to different speakers explained by the multiplicity of the abdominal air—the manifestor—which, arising from each respective speaker and independent of others, initiates a distinct auditory refinement (śrotra-saṃskāra) for each instance.

Because permanence and identity [of the sound] have been established by the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), just as the perception of multiplicity in the moon occurs due to the various retinal rays (*netravṛtti*) affected by cataracts (*timira*). Furthermore, designations such as "eastern" and so forth are justified in relation to the location of the manifesting speaker. The perception of short, long, and protracted [vowels] is likewise caused by the increase or decrease of the manifesting [articulation]. The perception of sound at a distance when with the wind, and its non-perception when against the wind, is also possible only on the view that sound is manifested;
for in those two cases, [respectively], there is the propulsion of the internal air from afar, and its obstruction.

Now, it may be argued that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not possible with respect to sound, because its manifestation is momentary. To explain: in the case of a crystal or similar objects, after the initial perception, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) arises; then, aided by that impression, the eye perceives "this is that very same [object]" immediately thereafter. In this case, however, the manifestation of the phoneme is momentary. Even if the auditory organ were eternal, once the manifestation has ceased following the arousal of the impression by that momentary manifestation, recognition ought not to arise subsequently.

It is said: The postulation of a cause is indeed in accordance with the effect. In this case, however, manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is not the awakener of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*); rather, when that [impression] is awakened by the force of causes such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), the very first manifestation itself is recognized as being of the nature of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). For example, in thick darkness, recognition is produced for a long-familiar object from the mere momentary flash of a lightning bolt. Therefore, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal. And all of this has been explained in detail in the *Nyāyaśuddhi*.

Thus, because the phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal and the meaning (*artha*) is eternal by way of its continuity, their relationship is non-human (*apauruṣeya*) due to being beginningless. For instance, the apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) of words by those seeking to acquire proficiency occurs today through the linguistic usage of elders of the present; likewise, it occurred for those who acquired proficiency previously through the usage of elders of the past; and likewise for those even earlier through their predecessors. Since this cycle of impressions (*saṃskāramaṇḍala*) has no first point, the succession of word and meaning is beginningless, and consequently, their relationship is also beginningless.

Furthermore, if sound were impermanent, there could be no linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) at all; for the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*) occurs through the linguistic usage of elders. And that [apprehension] would only be possible upon observing repeated usage, whereby—through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*) and the observation of repeated usage—one ascertains the individual meanings of the various words by excluding the meanings of other constituent parts. Indeed, it is impossible to observe the repeated usage of a sound that perishes immediately upon utterance.
Since such [repeated usage] would only be possible if sound were eternal, the proof of its eternity would thus also serve a purpose in facilitating linguistic acquisition.

This is the wish: that the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) might be beginningless. But that is not established. For instance, when the entire aggregate of effects has been withdrawn simultaneously, at the beginning of creation, the Supreme Person—the compassionate Lord of all, the All-Knowing and All-Powerful—having fashioned by means of his mind certain exceptional persons who are not born from a womb and are capable of the activities of creation, and having created the collection of primary elements and their derivatives (*bhūtabhautika*) differentiated into objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment, [he assigns them] to those respective purposes.

It is established by all means of valid knowledge that [the Lord], having established the convention that "this is the meaning of this word" and having revealed the Vedas, taught them to those persons; therefore, the relationship [between word and meaning] is of human origin.

This is not sound. While it may be granted that the creation and destruction of the class of effects occur sequentially, we see no evidence for their simultaneity. On the contrary, the following inference holds: the time under dispute (the present) does not possess the destruction of all effects, because it is time, like any currently perceived time. Alternatively: the destruction of a jar under dispute is always co-temporal with other jars, because it is a destruction, like the destruction of another jar.

Furthermore, if all effects were destroyed, then due to the destruction of the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) residing in all selves, there would be no diversity in subsequent creation. Passages such as, "In the beginning, indeed, this was nothing at all; there was neither sky, nor earth, nor the intermediate space," and likewise, "Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning—One only, without a second; having created that, it entered into it," are merely explanatory (*arthavāda*) and subordinate to injunctions; they are not capable of establishing a meaning independently, for the entire Veda [is authoritative only in relation to injunctions].

This is because the purport [of the scripture] concerns that which is to be practiced, and it will be explained that this is established through linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). Likewise, regarding the existence of an omniscient person: "The earth and so forth have an agent, because they are effects."

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the inference "like a jar" is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is pervaded by having a bodied agent (*śarīrikartṛkatva*); and since a bodied being cannot possibly be omniscient, while a bodiless being lacks the capacity to preside over causes, agency is impossible for the latter. Furthermore, since the succession of men in the present age is observed to be born from a womb, the existence of a man not so born is likewise inconceivable. All of this has been stated in the treatise titled *Vimalābjana*.

If it is argued that since the cognition of meaning based on convention is observed in words such as "Devadatta," it should likewise be the case for words such as "cow" (*go*), and therefore their lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) is untenable—it is not so. For in this case (the word "cow"), the convention is established through direct perception, whereas in other cases (proper names), there is no such [innate] convention because the acquisition of meaning arises solely from the usage of elders. If it is further argued that even in the case of words like "Devadatta," the cognition of meaning is sometimes seen to arise from convention—it is not so; for while the convention in those cases is arbitrary, the acquisition of meaning (*vyutpatti*) is fixed.

Therefore, in one case, denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) is based on the apprehension of power (*śakti*); in another case, however, even if denotative capacity is sometimes apprehended through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), it is based on convention (*saṃketa*). The perception of denotative capacity [in both cases] arises from the non-apprehension of any difference. Prior to convention, there is no perception of denotative capacity, just as there is none for words such as "cow" (*gavādi*). [Objection: If the relationship were not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), then upon hearing a word for the first time, everyone would simultaneously perceive its meaning without distinction. [Reply: This would not be the case, because linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) is also a necessary cause. Therefore, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal.

And it is established that the relationship [between word and meaning] is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). Its apprehension occurs through the apprehension of the expressive power (*vācakatva-śakti*); and that [power] is acquired from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), as will be explained.

Now, one might ask: how can there be a cognition of word-meanings or a cognition of sentence-meanings from words? Regarding this, the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas), who are experts in the true nature of speech-sounds, declare: since it is impossible for there to be a cognition of word-meanings or sentence-meanings through letters that are sequential, rapidly disappearing, and either individual or simultaneous, one must accept as the basis [of these cognitions] the reality of speech known as *sphoṭa*. This is designated by the terms "word" (*pada*) and "sentence" (*vākya*), is manifested by those respective letters, and is devoid of any division into letters. It is this [reality] that must be sought as the root.

For instance: there is no comprehension of meaning upon the apprehension of each individual phoneme, because that would lead to an over-extension (of the principle). Nor is there simultaneous apprehension, because of the extremely rapid succession [of their disappearance]. Therefore, the manifestation of the word (*pada*) occurs through a certain number of phonemes arranged in a fixed sequence; in this very way, the distinction between the meaning of a word and the meaning of a sentence is logically established.

Others, however, maintain that there is only one indivisible reality of speech (*śabdatattva*) in which the distinction between word and sentence has subsided; they hold that the division into words and sentences is merely conceptual.

Some maintain that this [word] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and must be inferred from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of meaning. Others, however, hold that it is perceptible by the sense of hearing. In the former case, the actual knowledge of words and word-meanings, as well as the actual knowledge of sentences and sentence-meanings, serves as auxiliary causes; in the latter case, it is the conceptual knowledge of words, their meanings, sentences, and their meanings [that serves]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of meaning occurring indiscriminately for everyone.

Furthermore, in cases such as "vananavanadīdīna," although there is a difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*), a difference in the words (*pada*) is perceived. Therefore, the word must be something distinct from those [phonemes]. Nor can it be argued that the phonemes themselves constitute the word, and that the difference in the cognition of the word in cases like "nadī" and "dīna" arises merely from a difference in their sequence; for since phonemes are all-pervading (*sarvagata*) and eternal (*nitya*), a sequence in space or time is impossible for them. Moreover, the designation of many phonemes as "one word" or "one sentence" is also proof that the word is distinct from the phonemes.

Furthermore, if phonemes were the denoters [of meaning], then a cognition of the meaning would occur even when there is a difference in their sequence, a difference in the speakers, or a delay in pronunciation; however, this is not sound. For even upon careful investigation, no partless linguistic essence (śabdatattva) is perceived apart from the various phonemes. As for the designation that "this is one word" or "this is one sentence," that too is based on the limiting condition (upādhi) of the unity of the object (artha). Indeed, a unity based on limiting conditions is observed even in the case of many things, as in the expressions "an army," "a forest," or "the Rājasūya sacrifice."

For this very reason, those who do not recognize the unity of meaning have no reflective awareness of that unity. For if the essence of the word were free from adventitious conditions (*anau-pādhika*), then it would be revealed both to those who are proficient through mere *saṃhitā* recitation and to others as well. If it is argued that proficiency (*vyutpatti*) is also a necessary auxiliary factor, and thus there is no over-extension [of the theory], then alas, this contradicts one's own experience; for a proficient person does not perceive that "this essence of the word is manifested by these phonemes."

Furthermore, since the capacity to denote a specific object is possible through as many phonemes as are required to manifest the essence of the word (*śabdatattva*), the postulation of anything additional is refuted by the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*). Even in cases such as *nadī* and *tīna*, the difference in cognition is based on the difference in sequence. For instance, due to the sequence of pronunciation, distinct cognitions arise corresponding to the manifestation of each individual phoneme.

Furthermore, due to the sequence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) known as cultivation, which is manifested by the perception of each individual phoneme, distinct recollections arise. By virtue of that sequence, the phonemes themselves appear as if they possess a sequence. Therefore, it is the phonemes alone—produced by a single utterance from the mouth, characterized by contiguity, endowed with a specific order, and possessing specific accents—that constitute the word (*pada*). From these alone arises the cognition of the meaning.

Nor is simultaneous apprehension impossible, because even those [sounds] heard in succession can subsequently become objects of memory in that very same order. Indeed, simultaneous recollection is observed even regarding things experienced in succession, as in the cases: "The five *prayāja* offerings were performed by me," and "I have bathed a hundred times in the great river Godāvarī. This point will be elaborated upon at the time of presenting our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

The postulation of a word that transcends the senses is also untenable, because the cognition of meaning is established otherwise. Furthermore, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): if it were eternal, there would be the consequence of the cognition of all meanings [simultaneously]; and if it were non-eternal, its cause would be difficult to determine. If the phonemes (*varṇa*) were its cause, their production would be useless, since the cognition of meaning is established by those very phonemes through the aforementioned process. If, however, they were its manifesters (*abhivyañjaka*), it would follow that it is perceptible.

Furthermore, linguistic proficiency arises from the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*) through the process of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*) within the usage of elders. Consequently, it is stated that the proficiency for a given word belongs precisely to that specific meaning-component which is inserted when that word is inserted, and deleted when it is deleted. However, in the theory of the indivisible word-essence (*akhaṇḍa-śabda-tattva-vāda*), what could possibly have proficiency in what? If it is argued that even there, proficiency is attributed to a word by postulating a division into constituent parts, we say no; this would involve excessive conceptual complexity (*pratipatti-gaurava*). For it has been stated that a "word" (*pada*) consists merely of phonemes (*varṇa*) arranged in a fixed sequence.

Furthermore, since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is established by this very reasoning, one need not postulate a "sentence" there and then claim that linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) occurs with respect to it; for even in that case, there would be a great deal of cumbersome effort in the process of understanding.
Thus, neither through perception nor through inference is there any possibility of a reality of sound (*śabdatattva*) distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*).

Others, however, maintain that since it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if each individual phoneme were the denoter of the word-meaning, and because phonemes perish so rapidly that they cannot be apprehended simultaneously, it is the final phoneme—assisted by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme—that denotes the word-meaning. Likewise, the final word—assisted by the mental impressions produced by the experience of each preceding word-meaning—denotes the sentence-meaning. They further assert that in this case as well, the actual acquisition of the relationship between words and their meanings (*padapadārthavyutpatti*) serves as a cooperative cause.

Furthermore, it is argued that this mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is distinct from the impression that causes memory, because the former is the cause of memory while the latter is caused by direct experience. This too is untenable, because the apprehension of meaning is established otherwise through the reasoning already stated, and because simultaneous apprehension has been demonstrated. Although here the distinction between word and word-meaning is real, nevertheless, the acquisition of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) must be explained with effort, since the final phoneme lacks the status of being a "word.

Likewise, the acquisition of proficiency regarding sentence-meaning is also [necessary], since the final word lacks the status of being a "sentence," and because in both cases neither [the first nor the last] is fixed.

Regarding this, the Neo-Naiyāyikas (Navīnas) maintain that word-meanings—whether denoted by words or merely recalled by them—when endowed with expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other conditions, convey the sentence-meaning. This too is untenable, due to the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating such capacities. To explain: under the theory of denotation (*abhidhāna*), there would have to be a capacity in the words to denote their respective meanings, and a separate capacity in those word-meanings to bring about the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

Likewise, since it is not observed that word-meanings cognized through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) produce the understanding of the sentence-meaning, whereas it is observed when they have been presented [by words], words bestow upon their meanings the power to bring about the understanding of the sentence-meaning. Their capacity to produce that [understanding] is another [power]. Now, one might object: even in the case of meanings cognized through other means of valid cognition, the capacity to convey a connection (*saṃsarga*) is indeed observed.

For instance, when someone has perceived whiteness through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) without knowing its substratum, has inferred a horse whose form was unknown by means of the sound of neighing, and has inferred a movement whose agent was unknown by means of the sound of the trampling of hooves, it is observed that he has the cognition, "A white horse is running," which consists of a synthesis (*saṃsarga*). As it has been said:
"For one who sees the white form and hears the sound of neighing, as well as the sound of the trampling of hooves, there arises the cognition: 'A white horse is running.'"
"It is observed that [the word] is devoid of a sentence."

[Objection: "The formless is of unmanifest form; that is to say, it has an unmanifest substratum. [Reply: Not so. For such a person, the very cognition of a connection does not arise; rather, some white object is seen, and only this much: "There must be a horse going along with someone else. Then, through proficiency gained from practice, one understands the sound of the hoof-stamping to be connected with a horse. At that time, the cognition "it is a running horse" arises solely from inference.

Now, when one determines that whiteness has as its substrate a horse inferred [by other means], even then, since it is not possible for it to reside in anything other than a horse, the cognition "the white thing is a horse" arises precisely through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). Likewise, if one infers that the whiteness whose substrate has been inferred shares the same substrate as running, then the cognition "the white horse is running" arises; otherwise, it does not. Thus, this [objection] is trivial.

Furthermore, if the mutual connection [of word-meanings] were understood solely from the comprehension of the individual word-meanings, then in which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would that [connection] be included? It cannot be in verbal testimony (*śabda*), because there is no employment of words [to convey that connection]. If, however, another means of valid cognition is admitted, then verbal testimony would be abolished. Therefore, one must postulate a capacity for the word-meanings presented by the words—never before seen elsewhere—to bring about the cognition of the sentence-meaning. Furthermore, since the words themselves must possess the power to instill that [capacity], there is the cumbersome complexity of postulating three distinct powers.

Now, is it not indeed a cumbersome assumption to accept that word-meanings possess the power to convey their mutual connection? [The answer is: A word-meaning denoted in an unconnected state indicates (lakṣayati) its connected state; for there certainly exists a relationship between a state and that which possesses the state. Thus say the venerable authors of the Vārttika:
"For in every case, the sentence-meaning is indeed indicated as that which is being indicated."

Others say that this is incorrect, [claiming] that this is not *lakṣaṇā* because it does not involve the abandonment of its own primary meaning (*svārtha*). For it is observed that *lakṣaṇā* occurs in cases such as the Ganges only through the abandonment of that primary meaning. They speak thus due to a deficiency in their study of Mīmāṃsā; for it is not the case that in every instance of *lakṣaṇā* the primary meaning is abandoned. To illustrate:

In the world, when it is said, "The umbrella-bearers are going," the word "umbrella-bearer" indicates the entire group consisting of both the umbrellas and those who carry them; yet the primary meaning of the word "umbrella-bearer" is not abandoned. Likewise, in the Veda, regarding the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," the word "Vaiśvadeva" indicates the group of deities known as the Vaiśvadevas; and its own primary meaning is not abandoned. For this very reason, others have accepted that there are two types of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), namely *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication involving both the abandonment and non-abandonment of the primary meaning).

Otherwise, a refutation is stated: indeed, *lakṣaṇā* (indication) occurs because the denoted meaning of the word "Gaṅgā" lacks syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the sentence-meaning; however, in cases such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), since the meaning of the word "cow" (*go*) does possess such connection, indication is improper. Furthermore, it is untenable for the sentence-meaning alone to be the indicated object.

Because there is an immediate cognition [of the sentence meaning] just as in the case of word-meanings, without the deliberation regarding the impossibility of a [direct] relation. Now, in that case, the position of [words] being mere reminders (smārakatva) would not involve any complexity: word-meanings, once reminded by the words, would lead to the understanding of the sentence-meaning. For instance, upon hearing a word, the word-meanings—experienced at the time of learning [the language] as being related to one another—are remembered. And when one member of a relation is perceived, there is a remembrance of the other member of that relation. As it has been said: "A word does not differ from a mere reminder, because it lacks any additional [meaning]."

"Because there is nothing additional"—that is, because there is no denotative function (*abhidhāyakatva*) other than that of reminding (*smārakatva*). This is incorrect, because it would follow that the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is not verbal (*aśābda*). For even the meaning of the sentence is indicated (*lakṣya*) by the word-meanings, but it is not denoted by the primary power (*śakti*). If it is argued: "Just as word-meanings are remembered by means of words, so too are the words themselves remembered by those [word-meanings], since there is no difference in their relationship; and thus, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is understood through the remembered words, which constitutes its being verbal (*śābdatva*),"—it is not so.

For there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress: first the hearing of the signifier, then the recollection of the signified, then again the recollection of the signifier, and then the recollection of that [signified] by means of those [recollections].

The Prabhākaras, however, maintain that the sentence is nothing other than the words themselves, and the meaning of the sentence is nothing other than the meanings of the words. In this regard, they assert that the words alone are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because words are understood to denote their own meanings as related to other meanings. To illustrate: such is the manner of acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) in the world at the outset. First, an elder (*uttamavṛddha*) employs the sentence, "Devadatta, bring the cow," whereupon a middle-aged person (*madhyamavṛddha*) proceeds to act.

At that time, the neutral observer who desires to acquire knowledge (vyutpitsu) thinks thus: "This person's activity is preceded by knowledge, because it is an activity, like my own activity; and that knowledge is produced by a sentence, because it occurs immediately after it. In this way, through repeated observation of usage, first of all a vague understanding of the sentence-meaning arises, namely: "The meaning of this sentence is the bringing of a cow."

Later, when at some point the sentence "Bring the horse" is uttered and one acts accordingly, through the insertion (*āvāpa*) of the word "horse" and its semantic connection, and through the removal (*udvāpa*) of the word "cow" and the lack of its semantic connection, a distinct linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) arises for each word: for the word "horse" in the sense of a steed connected with other meanings, and for the word "cow" in the sense of an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth, likewise connected with other meanings.

Thus, for a person who has become proficient through repeated observation of usage, but who previously did not understand the relationship between word and meaning, this doubt arises: "If it is a signifier, then it should have signified [the meaning] to me as well at the very beginning; if it is not a signifier, then it would not signify it even to an elder. In this way...

Furthermore, in one who doubts, this doubt arises: "Surely there must be some special quality in the elder from which he understands, whereas I do not. For one who desires a determination as to what that special quality is, it is the very capacity to convey meaning (*pratyāyakatva*) that constitutes the difference—since, through the usage of elders, one personally comprehends the meaning from those words. And that [capacity] is dependent upon the apprehension of the expressive power (*vācakatva-śakti*). And that apprehension occurs through the usage of elders.

The determination arises that "this [connection] did not exist for me previously, but it existed for an elder"; likewise, because there is no beginning for myself, for the elder before me, and for the lineage of elders preceding him, the naturalness of the relationship between word and meaning is established by its being non-human (apauruṣeya). Therefore, the capacity of words to convey meaning is inherent; and while this depends upon linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), it is not created by arbitrary convention (*saṃketa*). Furthermore, that convention is dependent upon the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word.

And that apprehension [of the word] occurs in the linguistic usage of the elder who is being prompted; that [usage] is rooted in the cognition of a qualified object; and since that cognition is rooted in the expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*) [of the word], it is inferred that the power itself has a qualified object as its domain. Furthermore, the processes of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*) have as their scope that which is already connected (*anvita*). Consequently, when it is said, "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), the word *go* (cow) conveys its own meaning as already connected [with the action]; the same applies to the word *ānaya* (bring). Therefore, because the apprehension of power occurs with respect to the connected, it is established that words denote that which is already connected (*anvitābhidhāyitva*).

Likewise, since the activity of middle-aged and elderly persons is preceded by the cognition of what is to be done (*kārya*), and since that [cognition] has its root in verbal testimony (*śabda*), it must be understood that all words have *kārya* as their primary purport. This [purport] belongs directly to suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) through the process of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*), whereas for other words it belongs through a mediated sequence; for the capacity (*śakti*) is grasped through those two processes for both the nominal stem (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) portions alike. This will become clear further below.

Indeed, the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of the related) cannot be established, because it is impossible to grasp the expressive power (*śakti*) in that which is related to [other meanings] due to the infinity of possible correlates (*pratiyogin*). Nor can one suspect a denotation of the related in a general sense, since from sentences one understands a specific relation. Furthermore, since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is possible even through the denotation of the mere individual forms (*svarūpa*), there is the additional fault of the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating an expressive power for *anvitābhidhāna*.

Is the expression of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) [effected] by another word denoting what has already been expressed, or by one denoting what has not yet been expressed? In the first case, that word also requires the meaning expressed by the first word as being related; and since that [first] word would likewise require the meaning expressed by the second word, there is a circular dependency (*parasparāśraya*). In the second case, the employment of other words would be redundant, and there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the cognition of all relations could arise from a single word alone. Not so—because the triad of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the rest serves as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). That is to say, when another meaning is expected, proximate, and capable of connection...

Because the apprehension of the word’s power (*śakti*) occurs with respect to that which is connected to it, what then is this "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*)? It is the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) on the part of the cognizer. What is its basis? Some say it is based on inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). For instance, since an action is invariably connected to its factors (*kāraka*), one who has heard of the action would have a desire to know the factor; likewise for the factor as well. That is incorrect, because the cessation of the desire to know would be impossible, since there is an infinity of word-meanings that are invariably connected to both [the action and the factor].

Therefore, the basis for this is precisely something else: the non-termination of the expression (*abhidhāna*) and the non-termination of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*). In cases such as "the door" (*dvāram*), when a single word is employed, the expression of the related meaning is not completed because the counter-correlative (*pratisambandhin*) has not been supplied; thus, when there is a desire to know that counter-correlative, the expression of the related meaning is completed by the addition of the word "be closed" (*saṃvriyatām*). This is also the case where, even when multiple words are employed, the expressed meaning does not reach its conclusion.

Just as in the case of the statement, "Devadatta is fat because he does not eat during the day," there is an expression of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) through the phrase "he eats at night" when there is a desire to know [the cause] of his eating at night; likewise, in the two sentences "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit" and "They perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña in the afternoon on the new moon day," there is an expression of the related meaning through the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) when there is an expectancy for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). The manner in which the person to be enjoined is sought shall be explained further below.

But surely, in this case, there would be no expression of the relatedness (anvitābhidhāna) by the words *śukla* (white) and *rakta* (red) in the sentences "Bring the white cow" (*gām ānaya śuklām*) and "The cloth becomes red with lac" (*raktaḥ paṭo bhavati daṇḍena*), because the sentence would reach its completion even without them? True, that is so when they are not employed; but when they are employed, since it is established through linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that all words uttered together function in concert, the force of the single sentence (*ekavākyatā*) gives rise to an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) directed toward those [words], and thus the expression of the relatedness occurs by means of them.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "But there is an expectancy toward the one who is impassioned. However, this is the distinction: in cases such as "The door," proximity (*sannidhi*) is postulated by virtue of expectancy; here, however, expectancy arises by virtue of proximity. For this very reason, they speak of a twofold nature of expectancy: that which is aroused (*utthāpitākāṅkṣā*) and that which is natural (*svārasikākāṅkṣā*).

Objection: Surely, proximity (*sannidhi*) and compatibility (*yogyatva*) alone would suffice as the defining characteristics of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*); what is the use of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)? Reply: Not so; for even when those two are present, we do not observe syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in the absence of expectancy. For example, in the sentence "This son of the king comes; let the man be removed," there is no mutual connection between the king and the man, because they lack expectancy for the son and the removal respectively. Furthermore, that expectancy does not arise simultaneously toward all correlates; rather, [it arises sequentially].

[The sequence of connection] occurs according to the fitness and order of those respective meanings, by way of the relationship between the primary and the subordinate. For instance, in the sentence "Bring the white cow with a staff," first there is a connection regarding the object (the cow), then regarding its qualifier (white), and subsequently regarding the instrument (the staff). Likewise, in the case of "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the connection must also be stated according to the sequence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). And regarding the determination of this sequence, the very cognition of worldly people is the authority. As it has been said in the *Vākyārthamātṛkā*:
"For the sake of denoting that which is already connected, or for the purpose of joining the meanings already stated..."
The desire for a counter-correlate is what is celebrated as "expectancy" (ākāṅkṣā).
Since even proximity is of no avail for one who lacks full competence,
expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) is also a necessary indicator for the acquisition of the meaning of words.
Just as the desire to know arises in a cognizer with respect to various related objects,
in that very same way, words denote their meanings as already connected.

Thus [it is said]. Now, what is "proximity" (saṃnidhi)? It is the transition to another meaning immediately after hearing a certain word, due to expectancy and semantic competency. And that [transition] is not based on the word alone, for we observe the expression of a related meaning even through a supplied (adhyāhṛta) element. If it is argued, "In that case too, it is the word itself that is supplied, and that word brings the meaning to mind," [we reply]: no, for the supply [of the word] occurs precisely by virtue of the impossibility of expressing the related meaning otherwise.

And since that [expectancy] is satisfied by the presentation of a suitable correlate (*pratiyogin*), it does not serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of a word. This has been stated in the section on Presumption (*arthāpatti*). Therefore, the expression of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) occurs with a word that is either presented by the text or supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*). Proximity (*sannidhi*) also arises only through sequence, like expectancy; as it has been said:

"In the case of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), proximity is merely born from words and is not a defining characteristic, for in common usage we observe a connection even with a meaning that is supplied by ellipsis."
The proximity of all counter-correlates does not occur simultaneously;
rather, this [proximity] proceeds sequentially, according to the sequence of the causal complex that brings about their presence.
In whatever manner the proximity of counter-correlates arises,
in that very same manner, through the words, there occurs a sequential comprehension of the related meaning.

In this context, expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and compatibility (*yogyatā*) are based on proximity (*sannidhi*). Even if something is proximate, if it lacks expectancy or is incompatible, it is displaced from its position in the Veda by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*). In common worldly usage, however, there is the risk of [uttering] irrelevant matters, meaningless speech, or statements at the wrong time; even when things are proximate, only what is recognized as such by worldly consensus is authoritative.

What, then, is this "fitness" (yogyatva)? That which is worthy of connection; and that is established by worldly means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). For that whose fitness is ascertained, there is a positive concomitance (anvaya); but for that which lacks it, there is none—just as in the case of fire and sprinkling in the statement, "One should sprinkle with fire. For this very reason, even if something is present in the Veda, if it is unfit, it is displaced from its context (prakaraṇa). In common worldly usage, however, such a case would result in a defeat (nigrahasthāna) on the grounds of shifting the subject matter (arthāntara) or other similar faults.

[Objection: In that case, how can there be an expression of words in the Veda as being related to the *apūrva* (the unprecedented transcendental result) as their object? For since that [result] is not within the scope of any other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), no fitness for a relationship with it is observed. [Reply: Even here, the determination of fitness in a general sense serves as the means for the comprehension of the specific relation; thus, there is no fault. That which is *apūrva* is indeed a "task" (*kārya*) itself; therefore, whatever is fit to be related to a worldly task is understood to be fit in the Veda as well. As it has been said:

"The fitness that is determined in the world by way of generality alone is the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) in the acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) regarding the expression of things as related."

Others, however, say: "That which has not been determined as incompatible is [considered] compatible; therefore, the denotation of the related meaning (anvitābhidhāna) is established even with a non-worldly (alaukika) meaning of the injunction. This is not correct; for just as compatibility is not determined regarding a non-worldly entity, so too would incompatibility [not be determined], and thus everything would be connected to everything in every way. Consequently, there would be no restriction such that only the verbal root-meaning (bhāvārtha) is connected as the object (viṣaya), and only those like one who desires heaven (svargakāma) qualified by non-prescribed attributes are connected as the persons to be enjoined (niyojya). Enough of this.

In some cases, even for those elements that are remote, a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is established by postulating proximity solely on the strength of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*). For example, the application of the *parṇatā* (leaf-cup) and other such details, which are taught as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*), occurs within the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*). By the force of reflecting upon fitness alone, there is a connection in a distinct manner—transcending the mode of connection through the well-known worldly relationship of action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*)—even for those enjoined with respect to the *apūrva*. Furthermore, although these are first connected by way of the word, there subsequently arises a cognition of their connection also by way of the meaning. Therefore...

Thus, in the *Āruṇādhikaraṇa*, although qualities such as redness (*āruṇya*) are first construed sequentially [with the substance], their subsequent connection with the substance occurs only indirectly (*pārṣṭhika*). Similarly, the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*), which is initially the object of cognition, is subsequently understood as the instrument (*karaṇa*); likewise, the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) and others, who are first construed with the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled), are subsequently understood as the qualified agent (*adhikārikartṛ*).

It should be understood that the three factors beginning with desire (ākāṅkṣā) are not merely causes for positive concomitance (anvaya), but rather a mutual relationship of cause and effect among them must be recognized through their respective instances of anvaya; thus, this path of reasoning is profound. Therefore, even though the counter-correlates (pratiyogins) are infinite, there is no impossibility of grasping the relation by resorting to a defining characteristic (upalakṣaṇa). For this very reason, there is no "denotation of the related" (anvitābhidhāna) in a general sense, because linguistic proficiency (vyutpatti) occurs in specific instances.

Now, it might be argued that there is complexity (gaurava) in the theory of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) due to the reliance on three limiting conditions (*upalakṣaṇa*); but this is not so, because even the proponent of the theory of "relation of the expressed" (*abhihitānvayavāda*) must necessarily accept them in order to establish a restricted relation. It is only word-meanings as characterized by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the other conditions that convey the relation, and no others; for it is precisely because of this that the power (*śakti*) resides in the related. Therefore, the view that words convey the meaning of the sentence by making the presentation of word-meanings their intermediate operation is refuted, since the meaning of the sentence is nothing other than the related itself.

If it is argued that even under the view of secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇapakṣa*), there would be infinite powers for the single word "cow" (*go*)—such as "bring the cow," "tie the cow," or "release the cow"—due to the infinity of the objects indicated, whereas under the theory of expressed connection (*abhihitānvayavāda*), there is only one power because of the unity of the meaning; we say no. For even when there is a difference in various correlates (*pratiyogin*), the distinction in the causal operation of making those correlates known is established by a single power whose object is the correlate that is required, proximate, and capable.

For example, the eye, by means of its single power of vision—which has as its object color, that which possesses color, and the substance inherent in them—is the cause of the distinction between various visual effects despite the difference in the counter-correlates (pratiyogin). Furthermore, this same inconsistency applies equally to the awakening of the connection with infinite counter-correlates, which are indicated by the expectancy for the name of the referent (padārtha) and so forth. Moreover, you yourself have stated that a suffix denotes its own meaning as conjoined with the meaning of the stem (prakṛti); the same applies to the stem as well. Consequently, every collection of words would function in exactly that manner; what is the point of this [unnecessary] distortion?

[Objection: "But even so, that which possesses relation (*anvayavat*) is not itself related (*anvita*). For the relation is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), while the other is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Consequently, since expressive power (*śakti*) must be admitted for both, there is the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*). [Reply: Not so. Possessing relation (*anvayavattā*) is simply being related (*anvitatva*); it is not...

The state of being related (*anvitattva*) does not acquire its own existence independently of the relation (*anvaya*). Indeed, just as a cloth does not exist apart from a pot, the state of being related does not subsist apart from the relation. Consequently, since it is impossible to cognize the state of being related without the relation, the cognition of that [relation] and the cognition of it [the state of being related] are one and the same. Power (*śakti*) extends as far as the relation, just like the individual instance (*vyakti*). For a universal (*jāti*) cannot be cognized apart from the individual instance; by the very nature of things, the cognition of that [universal] occurs only upon the cognition of the individual instance.

For [the universal] has the individual as its form (*ākāra*). Indeed, there can be no cognition of a form without an agent of that form. In that case, would not those two also be the object of a single power? No, it would not. Just as being possessed of a connection (*anvayavat*) is itself the nature of the connected, the nature of the universal (*jāti*) is not merely being possessed of an individual (*vyaktimat*); rather, the universal is distinct from the individual, for it has the individual as its form. Therefore, those two do not share a single power. In that case, would there not be a duality of powers for the cognition of both? No, it would not.

Even in the absence of a separate power (*śakti*), a universal (*jāti*) is perceived together with its individual (*vyakti*) solely by virtue of its own nature. For instance, a word denoting a universal cannot convey that universal without the individual, because it is impossible to perceive a form (*ākāra*) without that which possesses the form (*ākārin*). Therefore, since the word for the universal conveys the individual precisely by means of expressing the universal, no separate power need be postulated for it; this is according to the maxim that "the meaning of a word is not that which can be obtained through another means."

But even if they are both objects of a single cognition, why is one unnameable while the other is nameable? It is as follows: first of all, a linguistic convention (*saṅgati*) is impossible with respect to infinite individual instances (*vyakti*). Although it might be possible [to establish a convention] with respect to those [instances] qualified by the universal (*jāti*), even in that case, the word’s power (*śakti*) toward the universal must necessarily be admitted; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the universal being cognized from the word [directly]. Therefore, it is better that the power resides in the universal alone.

The denotation of the individual (vyakti), however, is obtained through its own nature as that which expresses the universal (jāti) due to parsimony; thus, there is no complete similarity with the example of the individual. Rather, the secret of the observation is this: the cognition of that [the individual] occurs only upon the cognition of that [the universal], and the non-cognition of that [the individual] occurs when that [the universal] is not cognized. Even if one were to somehow postulate two separate powers, the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna) is superior to the theory of the relation of the expressed (abhihitānvaya). For there would be three powers: the words’ power toward their own meanings, the meanings’ power toward the sentence-meaning, and again the words’ power toward establishing that [sentence-meaning].

In this case, however, there are two powers. Although there might be some degree of parity under the view that words merely cause recollection (*smārakatva*), nevertheless, for the sake of establishing that the sentence-meaning is verbal (*śābdatva*), it must be admitted that the power of the words themselves extends to the related meaning (*anvitagocara*). Furthermore, for this reason as well, the theory of denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) alone is logical; because, bypassing the words which occur first, [if one were to posit a power] in the word-meanings...

It is improper to assume that words possess the power to convey the meaning of a sentence as a whole. Furthermore, it is undisputed that words have the power to denote the meaning of a sentence, since this is accepted by you [the opponent]. Consequently, one must accept that very power as extending up to the related (anvita) meaning, rather than accepting a separate power for the word-meanings themselves; for the postulation of a property (*dharma*) is simpler than the postulation of a substratum (*dharmī*).
